children.title: Input Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Deviation between intended decisions and realized implementation inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Input Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncertainty between a selected design and its realized implemented input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathcal X\) be the nominal design selected by an optimizer, and let the implemented input be a random variable \(U\sim Q(\cdot\mid x)\). Input uncertainty is present when \(Q(\cdot\mid x)\) is nondegenerate, so the evaluated response is \(f(U)\), possibly with additional observation noise, rather than exactly \(f(x)\). The decision criterion consequently depends on the induced distribution of \(f(U)\) conditional on the nominal choice \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Input uncertainty occurs when the implemented design randomly differs from the nominal design chosen by the optimizer.
assumptions_latex: The nominal decision satisfies \(x\in\mathcal X\).
The realized implementation has conditional law \(U\sim Q(\cdot\mid x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Input uncertainty is present exactly when \(Q(\cdot\mid x)\) is nondegenerate for at least one relevant \(x\).

notation.meaning: implementation distribution conditional on the nominal design

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nominal-versus-implemented-input formulation is coherent, but the cited general stochastic-optimization section does not inspectably establish this specific meaning of input uncertainty or the nondegenerate-kernel criterion.

children.title: Controllable–Uncontrollable Separation
children.top_down_role: Distinction between decision variables and uncertain operating factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Controllable–Uncontrollable Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space separation of decisions from unrevealed exogenous variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic optimization model has controllable–uncontrollable separation when its arguments lie in \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal W\), the optimizer selects only \(x\in\mathcal X\), and nature generates \(W\in\mathcal W\) according to a prescribed law \(P_W\). The decision must be chosen without observing the current realization of \(W\), and choosing \(x\) does not alter \(P_W\). The resulting admissible objective is \(J(x)=\rho_{P_W}(G(x,W))\), with optimization performed over \(x\) alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The decision variable is selectable, while the environmental variable is generated externally, remains unrevealed at decision time, and has an unaffected distribution.
assumptions_latex: The response is defined on \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal W\).
The current realization of \(W\) is unavailable when \(x\) is selected.
The law \(P_W\) is invariant under the choice of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The separated problem is \(\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\rho_{P_W}(G(x,W))\), with no optimization over \(W\).

notation.meaning: performance functional under the environmental law

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record imposes the additional requirements that the environmental realization is unobserved at decision time and that its law is decision-invariant. Those restrictions are not inherent in every controllable–uncontrollable separation and are not inspectably supported by the cited general section.

children.title: Shift-Robust Search Regimes
children.top_down_role: Search behavior when deployment conditions or uncertainty laws differ from those learned.

children.title: Model-Shift Robustness
children.top_down_role: Search behavior when the learned surrogate structure becomes inaccurate.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Shift Robustness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Near-optimality uniformly over an admissible family of response models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a family of plausible response models and let \(R_m(x)\) be the loss of decision \(x\in\mathcal X\) under model \(m\in\mathcal M\). For \(\epsilon\ge0\), a decision \(\widehat x\) is model-shift robust over \(\mathcal M\) when \(\sup_{m\in\mathcal M}R_m(\widehat x)\le\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\sup_{m\in\mathcal M}R_m(x)+\epsilon\). Thus robustness concerns changes in the response model itself, while holding fixed the declared model family and loss convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision is model-shift robust when its worst loss across plausible response models is within a specified tolerance of the minimax value.
assumptions_latex: The model family \(\mathcal M\) is nonempty.
The robust value \(\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\sup_{m\in\mathcal M}R_m(x)\) is finite.
The tolerance satisfies \(\epsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model-shift robustness is certified by \(\sup_{m\in\mathcal M}R_m(\widehat x)\le\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\sup_{m\in\mathcal M}R_m(x)+\epsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epsilon-minimax condition is mathematically coherent and the condition kind fits the leaf, but no source is supplied for identifying this particular robust-optimization criterion with model-shift robustness.

children.title: Distribution-Shift Robustness
children.top_down_role: Search behavior when deployment uncertainty differs from the learned distribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Distribution-Shift Robustness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Near-optimality uniformly over an ambiguity set of data-generating distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty ambiguity set of probability distributions for uncertainty \(W\), and let \(L(x,W)\) be the loss of \(x\in\mathcal X\). For \(\epsilon\ge0\), a decision \(\widehat x\) is distribution-shift robust over \(\mathcal P\) when \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[L(\widehat x,W)]\le\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[L(x,W)]+\epsilon\). The ambiguity set specifies the distribution shifts against which the guarantee applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision is distribution-shift robust when its worst expected loss over a stated distribution set is nearly minimax optimal.
assumptions_latex: The ambiguity set \(\mathcal P\) is nonempty.
The loss \(L(x,W)\) is integrable under every \(P\in\mathcal P\) for relevant \(x\).
The tolerance satisfies \(\epsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distribution-shift robustness is certified by the displayed \(\epsilon\)-minimax inequality over \(\mathcal P\).

notation.meaning: loss under decision x and uncertainty W

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ambiguity-set minimax condition is a standard distributionally robust formulation and fits the leaf, but it lacks the required authoritative citation and locator.

children.title: Shift-Detection Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on identifying consequential changes from available observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Shift-Detection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic boundary for detecting a distributional change from finite samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be candidate pre-shift and post-shift laws, and let \(\phi:\Omega^n\to\{0,1\}\) be any test based on \(n\) independent observations. Its type-I and type-II errors satisfy \(P^n(\phi=1)+Q^n(\phi=0)\ge1-\operatorname{TV}(P^n,Q^n)\). Consequently, achieving both errors at most \(\alpha\in(0,1/2)\) requires \(\operatorname{TV}(P^n,Q^n)\ge1-2\alpha\). Below this separation, reliable shift detection is impossible without additional assumptions or observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two shifts cannot both be detected with small testing errors unless their n-sample distributions have sufficient total-variation separation.
assumptions_latex: The observations are independent under either \(P^n\) or \(Q^n\).
The test \(\phi\) is measurable.
The target error level satisfies \(\alpha\in(0,1/2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname{TV}(P^n,Q^n)<1-2\alpha\), no test has both type-I and type-II errors at most \(\alpha\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind and total-variation testing statement fit the terminal container, but the exact testing inequality and its convention for total variation require a specific authoritative source.

children.title: Resource-Aware Decision Models
children.top_down_role: Evaluation choices modeled jointly with cost, budget, time, replication, termination, and recommendation quality.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Sequential Decisions with a Fixed Budget; Cost-Aware Optimization and Termination as a Decision; Unknown Observation Costs
Information Acquisition Problems and Policy Families
Ranking and Selection: Efficient Simulation Budget Allocation

children.title: Resource-Constrained Utility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Decision models distinguished by the resource constraint and terminal objective.

children.title: Fixed Evaluation-Count Budgets
children.top_down_role: Search under a prescribed number of observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Evaluation-Count Budgets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential optimization constrained by a prescribed upper bound on the number of observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\in\mathbb N\) be prescribed before optimization. A sequential policy satisfies a fixed evaluation-count budget when it selects each \(x_t\) using only \(\mathcal D_{t-1}\), obtains at most one new observation per evaluation, stops after a total count \(T\le N\), and returns a recommendation \(\widehat x_T\) measurable with respect to \(\mathcal D_T\). If the protocol requires exhaustion of the budget, then \(T=N\). Performance may be evaluated by expected simple regret \(\mathbb E[f(\widehat x_T)-\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)]\) for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimizer may make at most N adaptive evaluations and then returns a data-dependent recommendation; protocols requiring full budget use stop after exactly N evaluations.
assumptions_latex: The prescribed budget satisfies \(N\in\mathbb N\).
Each completed evaluation consumes one count regardless of its location.
The recommendation \(\widehat x_T\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal D_T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The budget-feasibility condition is \(T\le N\); it becomes \(T=N\) only when full budget exhaustion is required.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

children.title: Fixed Monetary or Compute Budgets
children.top_down_role: Search under heterogeneous evaluation expenditure.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Monetary or Compute Budgets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility condition for sequential evaluations having heterogeneous, known or predicted costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a decision space, let \(c_t(x)>0\) be the resource charged for evaluating \(x\) after history \(\mathcal H_{t-1}\), and let \(B>0\) be a fixed budget. A sequential policy selecting \(x_t\) is budget-feasible through its stopping time \(\tau\) precisely when \[\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}c_t(x_t)\le B.\] If another evaluation would violate the constraint, the policy must stop; its terminal recommendation may be any \(\mathcal H_\tau\)-measurable decision, commonly the best evaluated point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A search is feasible when the total monetary or compute cost of all completed evaluations does not exceed the fixed budget.
assumptions_latex: \(c_t(x)>0\) is available or predictively specified when scheduling evaluation \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}c_t(x_t)\le B\).

notation.meaning: resource charge for evaluating x at stage t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the fixed-budget container, but the cited general stochastic-optimization section does not specifically support heterogeneous monetary or compute accounting. The formulation also blends costs known before launch with predicted costs: a predicted charge does not by itself guarantee the displayed realized-budget inequality. Moreover, one unaffordable evaluation does not force stopping when another affordable evaluation may remain. A source and formulation distinguishing known, reserved, and realized charges are required.

children.title: Deadline-Based Resource Accounting
children.top_down_role: Search quality governed by elapsed time and completion schedules.

children.title: Deadline-Limited Search
children.top_down_role: Optimization regimes governed by a fixed completion deadline.

knowledge_statements.title: Deadline-Limited Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility of sequential or parallel search under a hard wall-clock deadline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a deadline \(D>0\). For each launched evaluation \(i\), let \(s_i\ge0\) be its start time and \(R_i>0\) its realized runtime, so its completion time is \(C_i=s_i+R_i\). The information available for the terminal recommendation is generated only by evaluations satisfying \(C_i\le D\). A deadline-limited policy stops launching work according to its scheduling convention and outputs an \(\mathcal H_D\)-measurable recommendation at time \(D\); evaluations completing after \(D\) cannot affect that output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only evaluations completed by the fixed deadline inform the terminal recommendation; late results are unavailable to the decision.
assumptions_latex: \(D>0\) is fixed before search.
\(C_i=s_i+R_i\) records the realized completion time of evaluation \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat x_D\text{ is }\mathcal H_D\text{-measurable, with completed data restricted to }\{i:C_i\le D\}.\)
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports deadline-limited Bayesian search.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition matches deadline-limited search, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied. The conclusion also introduces \(\widehat x_D\) without assigning that symbol to the terminal recommendation in the statement. An authoritative source for hard-deadline information availability and a notation repair are required.

children.title: Wall-Clock Resource Accounting
children.top_down_role: Elapsed-time accounting across evaluations, queues, and coordination overhead.

knowledge_statements.title: Wall-Clock Resource Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elapsed-time accounting for sequential and parallel evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For evaluations with start times \(s_i\) and completion times \(C_i=s_i+R_i\), wall-clock consumption through termination is \[T_{\mathrm{wall}}=\max_{i\in I_{\mathrm{used}}}C_i-\min_{i\in I_{\mathrm{used}}}s_i.\] Under sequential, non-idling execution with negligible overhead this reduces to \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=\sum_{i\in I_{\mathrm{used}}}R_i\). Under parallel execution it is determined by the completion schedule rather than by the sum of runtimes, and therefore includes both concurrency and idle intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wall-clock cost is elapsed calendar time; it equals summed runtimes only for sequential non-idling execution without overhead.
assumptions_latex: \(I_{\mathrm{used}}\) is finite and nonempty.
\(C_i=s_i+R_i\) for every used evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=\max_{i\in I_{\mathrm{used}}}C_i-\min_{i\in I_{\mathrm{used}}}s_i\).
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports parallel wall-clock accounting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is locally appropriate, but no source is supplied. The displayed formula measures the span from the earliest used launch to the latest used completion, which equals wall-clock consumption only after the accounting interval and treatment of scheduling or terminal overhead are fixed. The phrase "through termination" is therefore broader than the formula without an additional assumption.

children.title: Completion-Schedule Risk
children.top_down_role: Terminal-quality exposure arising from uncertain completion schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Completion-Schedule Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chance-constrained control of failing to complete scheduled evaluations by a deadline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given launch decisions and possibly dependent random runtimes, let \(M=\max_{i\in I}C_i\) be the makespan of the scheduled evaluations. For deadline \(D>0\) and tolerance \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), the schedule has acceptable completion risk when \[\mathbb P(M>D\mid\mathcal H)\le\alpha,\] equivalently \(\mathbb P(M\le D\mid\mathcal H)\ge1-\alpha\). This probability must be computed under the joint predictive runtime law, since dependence and shared resource contention can change the tail of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A schedule is acceptable when its posterior probability of missing the deadline is at most the prescribed risk tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The joint predictive distribution of completion times conditional on \(\mathcal H\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(M>D\mid\mathcal H)\le\alpha\).
review_flags: No supplied source addresses probabilistic completion schedules or makespan risk.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chance constraint is a suitable condition for completion-schedule risk, but no source supports this particular makespan-risk formulation. The scheduled index set \(I\) should also be declared finite and nonempty, with completion times defined for all its members, before \(M=\max_{i\in I}C_i\) is used.

children.title: Open-Ended Cost-Penalized Search
children.top_down_role: Search balancing terminal quality against continuing expenditure.

knowledge_statements.title: Open-Ended Cost-Penalized Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indefinite-horizon search with terminal utility reduced by accumulated evaluation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau\) be a policy-chosen stopping time, \(\widehat x_\tau\) its terminal recommendation, \(U(\widehat x_\tau,\mathcal H_\tau)\) its terminal utility, and \(c_t>0\) the cost of evaluation \(t\). An open-ended cost-penalized search policy maximizes \[\mathbb E\!\left[U(\widehat x_\tau,\mathcal H_\tau)-\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}c_t\right],\] over admissible sampling and stopping rules, where \(\lambda>0\) converts resource expenditure into utility units. Unlike a fixed-budget regime, feasibility does not impose a predetermined finite evaluation total.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search jointly chooses evaluations and when to stop by trading expected terminal utility against accumulated resource cost.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda>0\).
\(\tau\) is a stopping time for the search filtration.
The displayed positive and negative utility components are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\pi}\mathbb E_\pi[U(\widehat x_\tau,\mathcal H_\tau)-\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}c_t]\).

source_refs.locator: 1.9 From deterministic to stochastic optimization p. 24

source_witnesses.locator: 1.9 From deterministic to stochastic optimization p. 24

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits open-ended cost-penalized search, and its mathematical objective is plausible. However, the cited introductory section does not specifically support joint sampling and optimal stopping with accumulated evaluation costs. The admissible policy class and conditions ensuring the objective is well-defined also need source-backed specification.

children.title: Cumulative-Reward Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings in which outcomes collected during search have operational value.

knowledge_statements.title: Cumulative-Reward Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential optimization where rewards obtained during experimentation contribute directly to performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For horizon \(T\), let a policy choose \(x_t\in\mathcal X\) from history \(\mathcal H_{t-1}\) and observe an integrable reward \(Y_t\) with conditional mean \(f(x_t)\). A cumulative-reward regime evaluates the policy by \[J_T(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}Y_t\right].\] If \(f^*=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)<\infty\), the equivalent expected-regret criterion is \(R_T(\pi)=Tf^*-J_T(\pi)\); maximizing cumulative reward is therefore equivalent to minimizing \(R_T\) for fixed \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every evaluation yields operational reward, so policy quality is total expected reward, equivalently cumulative regret against the best fixed action.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\) is fixed.
Each \(Y_t\) is integrable and satisfies \(\mathbb E[Y_t\mid x_t,\mathcal H_{t-1}]=f(x_t)\).
\(f^*<\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and reward-regret identity are mathematically consistent and fit the cumulative-reward container. The supplied locator is only the beginning of a broad learning chapter and does not specifically support cumulative reward or regret; the same inventory lists materially more specific cumulative-reward sections, but they were not cited. A supporting section or theorem locator is required.

children.title: Evaluation Resource Model Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Representations of expenditure, duration, availability, and completion.

children.title: Known Deterministic Costs
children.top_down_role: Costs available before scheduling and treated as fixed.

knowledge_statements.title: Known Deterministic Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation costs fixed by the candidate and known before scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be the set of admissible evaluations and \(c:\mathcal X\to(0,\infty)\). Costs are known and deterministic when scheduling \(x\) incurs the nonrandom charge \(c(x)\), known before launch and independent of objective observations, search history, and runtime noise. Consequently, for selected points \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), total charged resource is exactly \(C_n=\sum_{t=1}^{n}c(x_t)\), so budget feasibility can be checked before launching the next evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each candidate has a positive, preknown, nonrandom cost, making accumulated resource use exactly computable before scheduling.
assumptions_latex: \(c:\mathcal X\to(0,\infty)\) is known to the policy.
Scheduling an evaluation does not alter its charged cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n=\sum_{t=1}^{n}c(x_t)\text{ is known conditional on }(x_1,\ldots,x_n).\)

notation.meaning: known deterministic cost of evaluating x
total cost of n scheduled evaluations

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected definition fits the taxonomy leaf, but the cited section on deterministic optimization procedures does not specifically establish preknown evaluation charges. Determinism and prelaunch knowledge imply that \(c(x)\) is fixed conditional on \(x\), but independence from objective observations, history, and runtime noise is an additional modeling restriction that requires support or removal.

children.title: Learned Cost Model Family
children.top_down_role: Costs inferred alongside objective behavior.

children.title: Latent Cost Surfaces
children.top_down_role: Unknown expenditure patterns across candidate evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Latent Cost Surfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive, input-dependent evaluation costs modeled as an unobserved random function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be the evaluation domain. A latent cost surface is an unknown function \(c:\mathcal X\to(0,\infty)\) endowed with a stochastic-process prior and inferred from cost observations. A common positivity-preserving specification is \[g\sim\operatorname{GP}(m_c,k_c),\qquad c(x)=\exp(g(x)),\] with observations \(Z_i=g(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\) or noisy measurements of \(c(x_i)\). Conditional on accumulated data, the cost at an unevaluated point is represented by its posterior predictive distribution rather than a fixed known charge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation cost varies over the domain and is inferred as a positive latent function from observed costs.
assumptions_latex: \(m_c\) and \(k_c\) define a valid Gaussian process.
The cost-observation likelihood is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(x)=\exp(g(x))>0\text{ and }p(c(x)\mid\mathcal D_n)\text{ is predictive for unobserved }x.\)

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

review_flags: Locator supports surrogate search provisionally but may not explicitly discuss latent cost surfaces.

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A positive latent log-cost GP is a valid example of a latent cost surface and the definition fits the container. The cited optimization-and-search locator does not specifically support modeling evaluation cost as a latent process. In addition, \(\mathcal D_n\) appears in the conclusion without being defined in the statement or assumptions.

children.title: Online Cost Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Cost representations revised as expenditure observations accumulate.

knowledge_statements.title: Online Cost Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential updating of a predictive cost model from observed evaluation expenditures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an initial cost dataset \(\mathcal D_0\), a positive-cost probabilistic model \(p_0(c)\), and a stopping rule. At stage \(t\), fit or update \(p(c\mid\mathcal D_{t-1})\); supply its predictive distribution to the resource-aware selection rule; launch the selected \(x_t\); observe cost \(z_t\); and set \[\mathcal D_t=\mathcal D_{t-1}\cup\{(x_t,z_t)\}.\] Stop when the prescribed resource or decision condition holds, and output the final objective recommendation together with the current cost posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After every evaluation, update the cost predictor and use its predictive distribution when selecting and budgeting subsequent evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D_0\) and a cost likelihood are specified.
Each completed evaluation reveals a cost observation \(z_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(c\mid\mathcal D_t)\propto p(z_t\mid c,x_t)\,p(c\mid\mathcal D_{t-1})\).

notation.meaning: cost observations available after stage t

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

review_flags: Locator supports sequential surrogate search provisionally but may not specialize to cost observations.

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role is appropriate for this leaf, but the cited generic surrogate-search section does not support online cost-surrogate updating. The notation \(p_0(c)\) and the update formula also leave unclear whether \(c\) is a scalar cost, a latent function, or model parameters; a specialized source and internally consistent probabilistic model are required.

children.title: Objective–Cost Joint Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Statistical dependence between evaluation cost and objective behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective–Cost Joint Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint posterior modeling of objective value and resource cost, including cross-dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)\) denote latent objective value and \(g(x)=\log c(x)\) latent log-cost. Objective–cost joint uncertainty is represented by a joint posterior \(p(f,g\mid\mathcal D_n)\), not merely separate marginal posteriors. In a multi-output Gaussian-process model, \[\begin{pmatrix}f(x)\\g(x)\end{pmatrix}\sim\operatorname{GP}\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}m_f(x)\\m_g(x)\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}k_{ff}(x,x')&k_{fg}(x,x')\\k_{gf}(x,x')&k_{gg}(x,x')\end{pmatrix}\right).\] Nonzero cross-covariance permits an objective observation to update predicted cost and conversely; setting \(k_{fg}=k_{gf}=0\) gives the independent-prior special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint posterior captures dependence between objective values and costs; cross-covariance lets either observation update predictions of the other.
assumptions_latex: The block kernel is positive semidefinite.
\(c(x)=\exp(g(x))\) defines positive cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(f(x),c(x)\mid\mathcal D_n)\text{ retains objective--cost dependence through }k_{fg}.\)
review_flags: Supplied surrogate locator does not specifically establish multi-output objective–cost modeling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits objective-cost joint uncertainty, but no source is supplied for the multi-output Gaussian-process construction. Nonzero cross-covariance supports cross-updating under the stated joint Gaussian model and suitable observations; zero prior cross-covariance gives independent latent GP components, but posterior independence additionally depends on the likelihood and observation model. Those qualifications require source-backed formulation.

children.title: Cost-Learning Error
children.top_down_role: Decision sensitivity to inaccurate or poorly calibrated cost estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Learning Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predictive discrepancy of an online cost model and its effect on resource estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c(x)>0\) be the true cost and \(\widehat c_n(x)>0\) a predictor learned from \(n\) cost observations. Define log-scale pointwise error by \(e_n(x)=\log\widehat c_n(x)-\log c(x)\). If \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|e_n(x)|\le\varepsilon_n\), then every predicted cost obeys \[e^{-\varepsilon_n}c(x)\le\widehat c_n(x)\le e^{\varepsilon_n}c(x).\] Hence, for any finite proposed batch \(S\), its predicted total cost lies between the same multiplicative bounds on the true total cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform log-cost prediction error yields explicit multiplicative bounds on individual and batch resource estimates.
assumptions_latex: \(c(x)>0\) and \(\widehat c_n(x)>0\) on \(\mathcal X\).
\(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|e_n(x)|\le\varepsilon_n<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e^{-\varepsilon_n}\sum_{x\in S}c(x)\le\sum_{x\in S}\widehat c_n(x)\le e^{\varepsilon_n}\sum_{x\in S}c(x)\).
review_flags: The bound is elementary, but no supplied locator supports this selected cost-learning error formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically correct: a uniform log-error bound yields the stated pointwise and finite-batch multiplicative bounds. It also fits the cost-learning-error leaf. Nevertheless, no evidence record or source locator supports selecting this particular error definition and bound for the knowledge container, so source support is required.

children.title: Stochastic Completion-Time Models
children.top_down_role: Random evaluation duration and completion uncertainty.

children.title: Runtime Distributions
children.top_down_role: Probabilistic representations of evaluation duration.

knowledge_statements.title: Runtime Distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional probability laws for positive evaluation completion durations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an evaluation launched at candidate \(x\) under resource state \(r\) and history \(\mathcal H\), its runtime is a positive random variable \(R\) with conditional distribution \[F_R(t\mid x,r,\mathcal H)=\mathbb P(R\le t\mid x,r,\mathcal H),\qquad t\ge0.\] The associated survival function is \(S_R(t\mid x,r,\mathcal H)=1-F_R(t\mid x,r,\mathcal H)\). The model may be input-, state-, and history-dependent; a deterministic runtime is the degenerate special case in which this distribution concentrates at one positive value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime is modeled by a positive conditional distribution that may depend on the candidate, resource state, and observed history.
assumptions_latex: \(R>0\) almost surely.
The conditioning variables \((x,r,\mathcal H)\) are available when the predictive law is formed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_R(t\mid x,r,\mathcal H)=\mathbb P(R\le t\mid x,r,\mathcal H)\text{ and }S_R(t\mid x,r,\mathcal H)=1-F_R(t\mid x,r,\mathcal H).\)
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically treats conditional evaluation-runtime distributions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise, internally consistent, and appropriate for runtime distributions, but no source or locator is supplied. An authoritative probability, survival-analysis, scheduling, or resource-aware optimization source must support the conditional runtime-distribution formulation before candidate review can accept it.

children.title: Completion-Time Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty over when pending evaluations will finish.

assumptions_latex: Each evaluation is launched with a measurable configuration-channel pair \((x,a)\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal A\).
Completion occurs at an almost surely positive random time with a conditional distribution given \((x,a)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{x,a}\mid(x,a)\sim F_T(\cdot\mid x,a)\), with uncertainty summarized by this conditional law rather than a single deterministic duration.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines aleatoric completion-time uncertainty conditional on the selected evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \((x,a)\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal A\), completion-time uncertainty is a positive random variable \(T_{x,a}\) whose conditional distribution is
\[
F_T(t\mid x,a)=\mathbb P(T_{x,a}\le t\mid x,a),\qquad t\ge 0.
\]
A deterministic runtime model is the degenerate special case in which \(F_T(\cdot\mid x,a)\) is concentrated at one value. Conditional means or quantiles may summarize the law, but do not by themselves define its uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Completion time is modeled as a positive random variable whose distribution depends on the chosen design and evaluation channel, with deterministic runtime as a degenerate case.
knowledge_statements.title: Completion-Time Uncertainty

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Completion-Time Uncertainty leaf and is mathematically coherent, but it has no citation or inspectable locator supporting the conditional stochastic completion-time model.

children.title: Right-Censored Durations
children.top_down_role: Runtime information from evaluations not observed through completion.

assumptions_latex: A latent duration \(T_i>0\) and a censoring time \(C_i>0\) exist for each evaluation.
Only whether completion precedes censoring is observed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The observable pair \((Y_i,\delta_i)\) identifies an exact duration when \(\delta_i=1\) and the lower bound \(T_i>C_i\) when \(\delta_i=0\).

notation.meaning: latent completion duration and censoring time

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard survival-analysis representation of timeout-censored evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For evaluation \(i\), let \(T_i\) be its latent duration and \(C_i\) its censoring time. The right-censored observation is
\[
Y_i=\min\{T_i,C_i\},\qquad \delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}.
\]
If conditional noninformative censoring holds, the duration-model likelihood contribution at covariates \(z_i\) is
\[
f_T(Y_i\mid z_i)^{\delta_i}S_T(Y_i\mid z_i)^{1-\delta_i},
\]
where \(S_T(t\mid z)=\mathbb P(T_i>t\mid z_i=z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A timeout records the minimum of completion and censoring times plus an indicator; unfinished runs contribute survival probability rather than an exact duration.
knowledge_statements.title: Right-Censored Durations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and likelihood contribution are standard under conditional noninformative censoring and fit the Right-Censored Durations leaf, but no source supports the representation or likelihood formula.

children.title: Tail-Latency Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling regimes dominated by rare, unusually long evaluations.

assumptions_latex: The conditional survival function \(S_T(t\mid z)=\mathbb P(T>t\mid z)\) is defined for evaluation covariates \(z\).
A latency threshold \(u>0\) and tail probability level \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) are specified.
For the regular-variation classification, \(S_T(t\mid z)\sim L_z(t)t^{-\beta(z)}\) as \(t\to\infty\), where \(L_z\) is positive and slowly varying and \(\beta(z)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_T(u\mid z)\ge\alpha\) identifies substantial threshold exceedance, while regular variation distinguishes polynomial tails; under the stated tail equivalence, \(0<\beta(z)<1\) implies infinite conditional mean, \(\beta(z)>1\) implies finite conditional mean, and \(\beta(z)=1\) requires separate analysis of \(L_z\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes tail-latency regimes through threshold exceedance, upper conditional quantiles, and an explicitly stated regular-variation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At covariate \(z\), an \((u,\alpha)\) threshold-exceedance tail-latency condition is
\[
S_T(u\mid z)=\mathbb P(T>u\mid z)\ge\alpha.
\]
A complementary upper-quantile summary is
\[
q_{1-\alpha}(z)=\inf\{t:\mathbb P(T\le t\mid z)\ge 1-\alpha\}.
\]
If
\[
S_T(t\mid z)\sim L_z(t)t^{-\beta(z)}\quad\text{as }t\to\infty,
\]
where \(L_z\) is positive and slowly varying, then the tail is polynomially decaying. Under this equivalence, \(0<\beta(z)<1\) implies \(\mathbb E[T\mid z]=\infty\), \(\beta(z)>1\) implies \(\mathbb E[T\mid z]<\infty\), and the boundary case \(\beta(z)=1\) depends on \(L_z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail latency can be described by a substantial probability of exceeding a threshold, by an upper conditional quantile, or by a polynomial-tail model. For a regularly varying survival tail, exponents below one imply infinite mean, exponents above one imply finite mean, and the boundary exponent requires separate analysis.
knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Latency Regimes

children.title: Channel-Dependent Cost Models
children.top_down_role: Costs varying across candidate locations and information channels.

children.title: Input-Dependent Costs
children.top_down_role: Evaluation costs varying across candidate locations.

assumptions_latex: The design domain is \(\mathcal X\), and every evaluation at \(x\in\mathcal X\) consumes a nonnegative resource amount.
Expected cost exists wherever it is used for allocation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cost-aware decisions must evaluate the local function \(c(x)\), not a design-independent constant.

notation.meaning: random resource cost at input x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines costs varying across the design domain while holding the channel fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An input-dependent cost model assigns each \(x\in\mathcal X\) a nonnegative random cost \(C_x\) with conditional law \(P_C(\cdot\mid x)\). When integrable, its expected-cost surface is
\[
c(x)=\mathbb E[C_x\mid x].
\]
The model is genuinely input-dependent if there exist \(x,x'\in\mathcal X\) such that \(P_C(\cdot\mid x)\ne P_C(\cdot\mid x')\); variation only from repeated noise at a fixed \(x\) does not establish input dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An input-dependent model assigns different conditional resource-cost distributions to different design points; its mean cost is a function over the design domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Input-Dependent Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly separates input dependence from repeated cost noise and fits the exact leaf, but no cited source or locator supports this Bayesian-optimization cost model.

children.title: Source-Dependent Costs
children.top_down_role: Evaluation costs varying across information sources.

assumptions_latex: Evaluations may be requested from a finite or countable source set \(\mathcal S\).
Resource costs are nonnegative and conditionally distributed given the selected source.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selecting source \(s\) entails the source-specific law \(P_C(\cdot\mid s)\) and, when finite, mean cost \(c_s\).

notation.meaning: set of information or evaluation sources

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates cost variation by information source from variation by design input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A source-dependent cost model associates each source \(s\in\mathcal S\) with a nonnegative conditional cost law \(P_C(\cdot\mid s)\). If \(C_s\) is integrable, define
\[
c_s=\mathbb E[C_s\mid s].
\]
The model is source-dependent when \(P_C(\cdot\mid s)\ne P_C(\cdot\mid s')\) for some \(s\ne s'\). If cost also varies with input, the appropriate law is \(P_C(\cdot\mid x,s)\), and source dependence is assessed with \(x\) fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each information source has its own conditional cost distribution and mean; source dependence is assessed separately from input dependence.
knowledge_statements.title: Source-Dependent Costs

children.title: Fidelity-Dependent Costs
children.top_down_role: Evaluation costs varying across accuracy or resolution levels.

assumptions_latex: Fidelity belongs to an ordered set \((\mathcal R,\preceq)\).
Every evaluation at fidelity \(r\in\mathcal R\) incurs a nonnegative, integrable cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fidelity-dependent model uses \(c(r)\), commonly constrained to be nondecreasing under \(\preceq\).

notation.meaning: random evaluation cost at fidelity r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines resource cost as a function of an ordered fidelity parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A fidelity-dependent cost model assigns each \(r\in\mathcal R\) a nonnegative random cost \(C_r\) and expected cost
\[
c(r)=\mathbb E[C_r\mid r].
\]
When \(r\preceq r'\) means that \(r'\) is at least as accurate or resource intensive as \(r\), the usual monotone-cost condition is \(c(r)\le c(r')\). Fidelity dependence itself requires only that the conditional cost law vary with \(r\), not that monotonicity hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation cost varies with fidelity. Higher fidelity is often assumed no cheaper, although fidelity dependence alone does not imply monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.title: Fidelity-Dependent Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition appropriately distinguishes fidelity dependence from the optional monotone-cost condition and fits the leaf, but it lacks an authoritative citation and locator.

children.title: Cross-Channel Cost Interactions
children.top_down_role: Cost variation created by interactions among inputs, sources, and fidelities.

assumptions_latex: A joint channel \(a=(s,r)\) combines source \(s\in\mathcal S\) and fidelity \(r\in\mathcal R\).
The conditional mean cost \(c(s,r)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero interaction contrast means source and fidelity effects cannot be represented by additive main effects alone.

notation.meaning: conditional expected cost for source s and fidelity r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses an additive-separability test for interactions between two channel coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For sources \(s,s'\in\mathcal S\) and fidelities \(r,r'\in\mathcal R\), define
\[
\Delta_c(s,s';r,r')=c(s,r)-c(s,r')-c(s',r)+c(s',r').
\]
There is a cross-channel cost interaction exactly when \(\Delta_c(s,s';r,r')\ne0\) for at least one quadruple. If every such contrast vanishes on a Cartesian channel domain, then there exist functions \(u\) and \(v\) such that \(c(s,r)=u(s)+v(r)\), up to an arbitrary additive normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Source and fidelity costs interact when changing fidelity has a different cost effect across sources, detected by a nonzero four-point contrast.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Channel Cost Interactions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The four-point contrast is a valid condition for failure of additive separability on a Cartesian source-fidelity domain, and `condition` fits this leaf. No source or locator supports the characterization.

children.title: Dynamic Resource Capacity Models
children.top_down_role: Evaluation opportunities governed by changing availability or capacity.

children.title: Temporal Availability Profiles
children.top_down_role: Evaluation opportunities that change over time.

assumptions_latex: Time ranges over a horizon \([0,H]\), and resource capacity is represented in \(d\) nonnegative coordinates.
The availability process is measurable and integrable over the horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The profile \(A(t)\) determines instantaneous availability and \(B(t_0,t_1)\) determines cumulative available resource over any interval.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines deterministic or stochastic time-indexed resource availability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A temporal availability profile is a measurable process
\[
A:[0,H]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R_+^d,
\]
where \(A_j(t)\) is the capacity of resource \(j\) available at time \(t\). Its cumulative availability on \([t_0,t_1]\subseteq[0,H]\) is
\[
B(t_0,t_1)=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}A(t)\,dt.
\]
A deterministic schedule is obtained when \(A(t)\) is nonrandom; otherwise its conditional law given current information specifies availability uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A temporal profile gives the available capacity of each resource over time; integration yields cumulative capacity on any interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Temporal Availability Profiles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The time-indexed capacity process and its integral fit Temporal Availability Profiles, but no source is cited for this dynamic-capacity representation.

children.title: Capacity-Constrained Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Search under limits on simultaneous or cumulative resource use.

assumptions_latex: At time \(t\), active or newly admitted evaluations form a set \(J(t)\).
Each evaluation \(i\) requests a nonnegative resource vector \(r_i(t)\), and available capacity is \(A(t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An evaluation schedule is feasible only if aggregate demand never exceeds available capacity componentwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the componentwise feasibility constraint for concurrently running evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A schedule of evaluations is capacity-feasible on \([0,H]\) if, for almost every \(t\in[0,H]\),
\[
\sum_{i\in J(t)}r_i(t)\le A(t)
\]
componentwise. An admission decision for a new evaluation with demand \(r_{\mathrm{new}}(t)\) is feasible only when replacing \(J(t)\) by \(J(t)\cup\{\mathrm{new}\}\) preserves this inequality throughout its planned execution interval. Under uncertain capacity, feasibility may instead be imposed almost surely or at a specified chance level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concurrent evaluations are feasible only when their total demand does not exceed each available resource capacity throughout execution.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Constrained Evaluation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The componentwise deterministic feasibility condition is precise and the `condition` kind fits the leaf. The almost-sure and chance-constrained extensions are only mentioned rather than specified, and no source supports either the core condition or those variants.

children.title: Resource Contention
children.top_down_role: Competition among evaluations for shared capacity.

assumptions_latex: Multiple active evaluations share a finite-capacity scalar resource.
Each evaluation \(i\) has a service requirement \(w_i>0\) and receives a measurable, nonnegative service rate \(v_i(t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Contention is present when shared loading reduces some service allocation below its isolated allocation on a set of positive measure; the resulting completion time is determined by accumulated service.

notation.meaning: service rate allocated to evaluation i
isolated service rate of evaluation i
completion time of evaluation i under accumulated service

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines contention through reduced service allocation under simultaneous demand for a shared scalar resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let evaluation \(i\) require total service \(w_i>0\), receive a measurable rate \(v_i(t)\ge0\), and have completion time
\[
T_i=\inf\left\{t\ge0:\int_0^t v_i(u)\,du\ge w_i\right\}.
\]
Resource contention occurs when simultaneous demand forces \(v_i(t)<v_i^{0}(t)\) on a set of positive measure for some \(i\), where \(v_i^{0}(t)\) is its isolated service rate. For a shared scalar resource with capacity \(A(t)\), the allocations must satisfy
\[
\sum_i v_i(t)\le A(t)
\]
for almost every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evaluation completes after receiving its required accumulated service. Contention occurs when simultaneous evaluations reduce at least one service rate below its isolated rate while their total allocation remains within shared capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource Contention

children.title: Availability Forecast Error
children.top_down_role: Scheduling sensitivity to inaccurate forecasts of future resources.

assumptions_latex: A forecast \(\widehat A_{t\mid s}\) made at time \(s\) predicts future capacity \(A_t\).
Both forecast and realized capacity lie in \(\mathbb R^d\) and have finite second moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Forecast error is the realized-minus-predicted vector; its conditional mean measures bias, and its centered conditional second moment is its conditional covariance.

notation.meaning: capacity forecast made at time s

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines point-forecast error and its conditional first two centered moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(0\le s<t\le H\), the availability forecast error is
\[
e_{t\mid s}=A_t-\widehat A_{t\mid s}.
\]
Relative to the information \(\mathcal F_s\) available when the forecast is issued, define
\[
\mu_{t\mid s}=\mathbb E[e_{t\mid s}\mid\mathcal F_s].
\]
The forecast is conditionally unbiased when \(\mu_{t\mid s}=0\). Its conditional error covariance is
\[
\Sigma_{t\mid s}=\mathbb E\!\left[(e_{t\mid s}-\mu_{t\mid s})(e_{t\mid s}-\mu_{t\mid s})^{\mathsf T}\mid\mathcal F_s\right].
\]
A nonzero \(\mu_{t\mid s}\) represents conditional forecast bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Availability forecast error is realized capacity minus predicted capacity. Its conditional mean measures bias, and the centered conditional second moment gives its conditional covariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Availability Forecast Error

children.title: Adaptive Effort Allocation
children.top_down_role: Allocation of finite simulation or experimental effort across candidates and observation channels.

children.title: New-Point versus Replication Decisions
children.top_down_role: Allocation between exploring new candidates and reducing uncertainty at existing ones.

assumptions_latex: At decision stage \(n\), observations \(\mathcal D_n\) induce a posterior distribution over the unknown objective.
The action set contains evaluations at new locations and replications of previously sampled locations.
Each action has a positive expected cost, a defined one-step expected posterior value, and must satisfy the remaining-budget constraint before selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy selects a budget-feasible action maximizing \(V_n(a)/c_n(a)\); a replicate is forced only when its best score is strictly greater than the best score among feasible new-point actions, while equality permits either action type.

notation.meaning: one-step expected posterior value of action a
expected resource cost of action a
remaining resource budget at stage n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies one generic cost-normalized, one-step policy for allocating effort between new points and replications; it is not asserted to be the unique valid policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given data \(\mathcal D_n\), sampled-location set \(X_n\), and remaining budget \(b_n\), form
\[
\mathcal A_n=\{\operatorname{new}(x):x\in\mathcal X\setminus X_n\}\cup\{\operatorname{rep}(x):x\in X_n\}.
\]
For each \(a\in\mathcal A_n\), let \(V_n(a)\ge0\) be its specified one-step expected posterior value and let \(c_n(a)>0\) be its expected cost. Restrict selection to
\[
\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{feas}}=\{a\in\mathcal A_n:c_n(a)\le b_n\}.
\]
If \(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{feas}}\ne\varnothing\), select
\[
a_n\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{feas}}}\frac{V_n(a)}{c_n(a)},
\]
observe the resulting evaluation, and update \(\mathcal D_{n+1}\) and the remaining budget. If \(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{feas}}=\varnothing\), stop and output the posterior-recommended design. A replication is the unique action type selected only when the best feasible replication score is strictly greater than the best feasible new-point score; equality requires a tie-breaking rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each stage, compare budget-feasible new evaluations and replications by a specified expected posterior value per expected cost. Choose a maximizing action, update the posterior and budget, and stop when no action is affordable; tied action types require a tie-breaking rule.
knowledge_statements.title: New-Point versus Replication Decisions

children.title: Variance-Aware Replication Allocation
children.top_down_role: Replication effort adapted to heterogeneous observation variability.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Aware Replication Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy replication for independent heteroscedastic sample-mean estimators under evaluation costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let alternatives be indexed by \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Replication \(r\) at alternative \(i\) returns an independent observation with mean \(f_i\), variance \(\tau_i^2\), and cost \(c_i>0\). Initialize with \(n_i\geq 1\) observations and remaining budget \(b\). While some \(c_i\leq b\), select
\[i^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i:c_i\leq b}\frac{\tau_i^2}{c_i n_i(n_i+1)},\]
obtain one replication at \(i^*\), set \(n_{i^*}\leftarrow n_{i^*}+1\), and set \(b\leftarrow b-c_{i^*}\). Stop when no replication is affordable and return the sample means and replication counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly sample the affordable alternative giving the largest reduction in sample-mean variance per unit cost, then stop when no replication is affordable.
assumptions_latex: \(m<\infty\), \(n_i\geq 1\), and \(c_i>0\) for every alternative.
Observations are independent with finite, known variances \(\tau_i^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[i^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i:c_i\leq b}\frac{\tau_i^2}{c_i n_i(n_i+1)}.\]

notation.meaning: Current replication count at alternative i.
Per-replication observation variance at alternative i.
Cost of one replication at alternative i.

review_flags: Exact heteroscedastic variance-reduction allocation requires a directly supporting source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variance-reduction expression is mathematically consistent for independent sample means with known per-replication variances, and the algorithm fits the leaf. However, no inspectable source supports this exact greedy heterogeneous-cost allocation policy.

children.title: Sequential Elimination Allocation
children.top_down_role: Concentration of effort after removing weak alternatives.

children.title: Screening-Based Allocation
children.top_down_role: Early resource allocation used to assess a broad candidate set.

knowledge_statements.title: Screening-Based Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential confidence-bound screening for finite-alternative minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_0=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). At stage \(t\), construct simultaneous confidence intervals \([L_{i,t},U_{i,t}]\) for every \(i\in A_t\). Retain
\[A_{t+1}=\left\{i\in A_t:L_{i,t}\leq\min_{j\in A_t}U_{j,t}\right\}.\]
If \(|A_{t+1}|=1\) or no evaluation is affordable, stop and return any member minimizing \(U_{i,t}\). Otherwise allocate the next affordable evaluation among \(A_{t+1}\) to an alternative maximizing the predicted decrease in interval radius per unit cost, update the intervals, and repeat. Eliminated alternatives receive no further evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard alternatives whose lower confidence bound exceeds a surviving competitor’s upper bound, then allocate further effort only among unscreened alternatives.
assumptions_latex: The alternative set is finite and the objective is minimized.
At each stage, simultaneous confidence intervals are available for all active alternatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[A_{t+1}=\left\{i\in A_t:L_{i,t}\leq\min_{j\in A_t}U_{j,t}\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Confidence interval for alternative i at stage t.

review_flags: A source for the precise sequential screening and allocation rule is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The screening set is consistent with minimization, but the interval-radius-per-cost allocation rule and the terminal recommendation rule are presented as a specific algorithm without a source. The return statement should also specify that minimization is over the surviving set.

children.title: Elimination-Based Reallocation
children.top_down_role: Concentration of remaining effort after candidate removal.

knowledge_statements.title: Elimination-Based Reallocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reallocation of planned evaluations after irreversible elimination of alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At stage \(t\), let \(A_t\) be the active alternatives, let \(E_t\subseteq A_t\) be those eliminated by a valid screening rule, and let \(k_i\geq0\) denote evaluations previously planned for alternative \(i\). Form \(A_{t+1}=A_t\setminus E_t\) and the released effort \(K_t=\sum_{i\in E_t}k_i\). Given nonnegative priorities \(q_{j,t}\) on \(A_{t+1}\) with positive sum, assign each survivor the additional integer allocation obtained by rounding
\[K_t\frac{q_{j,t}}{\sum_{\ell\in A_{t+1}}q_{\ell,t}},\]
with residual evaluations distributed by largest fractional remainders. No eliminated alternative receives further effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pool evaluations released by eliminated alternatives and redistribute them among survivors in proportion to current nonnegative priorities, preserving the total planned effort.
assumptions_latex: \(E_t\subseteq A_t\) is supplied by an irreversible elimination rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[A_{t+1}=A_t\setminus E_t,\qquad \sum_{j\in A_{t+1}}k^{\mathrm{add}}_{j,t}=\sum_{i\in E_t}k_i.\]

notation.meaning: Total evaluation effort released by elimination.
Reallocation priority of surviving alternative j.

review_flags: The proportional integer reallocation convention needs a direct allocation-method source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proportional largest-remainder construction fits elimination-based reallocation, but no source supports this exact convention. Moreover, the claimed integer conservation requires the planned counts k_i, and hence K_t, to be nonnegative integers rather than merely nonnegative numbers.

children.title: False-Elimination Risk
children.top_down_role: Loss of strong candidates through premature screening decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: False-Elimination Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Familywise risk bound for confidence-based sequential elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the true minimizer \(i^*\) is unique. At each stage \(t\), elimination uses intervals \([L_{i,t},U_{i,t}]\) and removes \(i\) only when \(L_{i,t}>\min_{j\in A_t}U_{j,t}\). If the simultaneous coverage failure probability at stage \(t\) is at most \(\alpha_t\), then elimination of \(i^*\) can occur only after a coverage failure. Consequently, for any finite or countable sequence of stages,
\[\mathbb P\!\left(i^*\text{ is ever eliminated}\right)\leq\sum_{t\geq0}\alpha_t.\]
Thus choosing summable error spending with total at most \(\alpha\) controls false elimination by \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under simultaneous confidence coverage, the true minimizer cannot be screened out; a union bound limits its probability of ever being eliminated by total error spending.
assumptions_latex: The minimizer \(i^*\) is unique.
Stagewise simultaneous interval failure probabilities satisfy \(\mathbb P(F_t)\leq\alpha_t\).
The elimination rule removes \(i\) only if \(L_{i,t}>\min_{j\in A_t}U_{j,t}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathbb P\!\left(i^*\text{ is ever eliminated}\right)\leq\sum_{t\geq0}\alpha_t.\]

notation.meaning: Failure of simultaneous interval coverage at stage t.

review_flags: The union-bound argument is standard, but a sequential-elimination source is still required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The familywise union bound is correct under simultaneous coverage of all active alternatives at each stage, and property is an appropriate content kind. A sequential-elimination source with a specific locator is still required for this nontrivial risk statement.

children.title: Cost-Aware Policy Families
children.top_down_role: Acquisition families accounting explicitly for unequal expenditure.

children.title: Utility-per-Cost Policies
children.top_down_role: One-step utilities normalized or traded against evaluation cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Utility-per-Cost Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step selection by expected utility gain normalized by deterministic evaluation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_t\) be the current information state, \(A_t\) the feasible actions, \(c_t(a)>0\) the deterministic cost of action \(a\), and \(U_t(a)\geq0\) its conditional expected one-step utility gain. Given remaining budget \(b_t\), choose
\[a_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in A_t:\,c_t(a)\leq b_t}\frac{U_t(a)}{c_t(a)}.\]
Observe the action outcome, update \(D_{t+1}\), and set \(b_{t+1}=b_t-c_t(a_t)\). Stop when no action is affordable or every affordable action has zero utility; output the terminal recommendation prescribed by the decision model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among affordable actions, select the largest conditional expected one-step utility gain per unit cost and continue until no positive-utility action is affordable.
assumptions_latex: \(A_t\) is nonempty before termination and \(c_t(a)>0\).
\(U_t(a)\) is measurable with respect to the current information state and is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[a_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a:c_t(a)\leq b_t}\frac{U_t(a)}{c_t(a)}.\]
review_flags: A direct source for generic utility-per-cost normalization is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated utility-per-cost policy matches the leaf and is internally coherent, but the exact generic normalization, stopping rule, and terminal behavior have no cited support.

children.title: Cost-Aware Knowledge-Gradient Policies
children.top_down_role: Terminal decision value assessed under heterogeneous costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Aware Knowledge-Gradient Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-alternative knowledge gradient normalized by heterogeneous observation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite alternatives, let \(\mu_t(i)=\mathbb E[f_i\mid D_t]\), let action \(a\) produce observation \(Y_a\), and let \(c(a)>0\). For minimization define the knowledge gradient
\[\operatorname{KG}_t(a)=\min_i\mu_t(i)-\mathbb E_t\!\left[\min_i\mu_{t+1}(i)\mid a\right].\]
Among actions affordable under remaining budget \(b_t\), select
\[a_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a:c(a)\leq b_t}\frac{\operatorname{KG}_t(a)}{c(a)}.\]
Update the posterior after observing \(Y_{a_t}\), debit its cost, and repeat. At termination recommend an alternative minimizing the posterior mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the affordable observation with the largest expected improvement in terminal posterior-mean decision value per unit cost, then recommend the smallest posterior mean.
assumptions_latex: The alternative and action sets are finite.
Posterior means and the displayed conditional expectations are finite.
Observation costs are deterministic and strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[a_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a:c(a)\leq b_t}\frac{\operatorname{KG}_t(a)}{c(a)}.\]

notation.meaning: Posterior mean objective value of alternative i.
Expected one-step improvement in terminal decision value.

The cited section supports discrete-alternative knowledge gradient, but the supplied evidence does not establish heterogeneous-cost normalization or the complete budgeted policy; full-text confirmation or a cost-aware KG source is required.

children.title: Cost-Aware Information Search
children.top_down_role: Information-based policies that price observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Aware Information Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information acquisition priced by the cost of each observation action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\) be a decision-relevant latent quantity, \(D_t\) the current data, and \(Y_a\) the prospective outcome of action \(a\) with cost \(c(a)>0\). Define conditional information gain
\[I_t(a)=I(Z;Y_a\mid D_t)=H(Z\mid D_t)-\mathbb E_t[H(Z\mid D_t,Y_a)].\]
With remaining budget \(b_t\), choose an affordable action satisfying
\[a_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a:c(a)\leq b_t}\frac{I_t(a)}{c(a)}.\]
Observe \(Y_{a_t}\), update the conditional distribution, debit the cost, and repeat until no action with positive information gain is affordable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select the affordable observation giving the largest conditional mutual information about a decision-relevant latent quantity per unit cost.
assumptions_latex: The conditional entropies defining \(I_t(a)\) exist and are finite.
Every available action has deterministic cost \(c(a)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[a_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a:c(a)\leq b_t}\frac{I(Z;Y_a\mid D_t)}{c(a)}.\]

notation.meaning: Conditional mutual information supplied by action a.

review_flags: A source connecting conditional information gain with cost-normalized Bayesian search is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional mutual-information formula and cost-normalized selection rule are coherent and match the leaf, but no source supports their combination as the stated Bayesian search algorithm.

children.title: Budgeted Nonmyopic Policies
children.top_down_role: Lookahead policies accounting for downstream resource allocation.

assumptions_latex: The information state belongs to a measurable state space, the feasible action set is \(A(D,b)=\{a:c(a)\leq b\}\), and each action cost satisfies \(c(a)>0\).
The terminal value \(g(D)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb E[u(x,\theta)\mid D]\) and all displayed conditional continuation values are finite.
The required suprema admit measurable maximizing selections whenever an action or terminal recommendation is chosen.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[V(D,b)=\max\left\{g(D),\sup_{a\in A(D,b)}\mathbb E\!\left[V(T(D,a,Y_a),b-c(a))\mid D,a\right]\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Optimal value at information state D with remaining budget b.
Optimal value of stopping and selecting a terminal recommendation.
Information-state update after action a and observation Y_a.

review_flags: The cited lookahead section requires full-text confirmation for the exact remaining-budget Bellman recursion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-budget Bellman policy with observation costs and an explicitly defined terminal recommendation value.

source_refs.locator: 1.6.2 Policies based on lookahead approximations p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be an information state, let \(b\geq0\) be the remaining budget, let \(\mathcal X\) be the terminal recommendation set, and define the value of stopping by \(g(D)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb E[u(x,\theta)\mid D]\). For an observation action \(a\) with cost \(c(a)>0\), prospective outcome \(Y_a\), and state transition \(T(D,a,Y_a)\), let \(A(D,b)=\{a:c(a)\leq b\}\). If \(A(D,b)=\varnothing\), set \(V(D,b)=g(D)\). Otherwise define
\[V(D,b)=\max\left\{g(D),\sup_{a\in A(D,b)}\mathbb E\!\left[V(T(D,a,Y_a),b-c(a))\mid D,a\right]\right\}.\]
Stop when the first term attains the maximum; otherwise choose an affordable action attaining the continuation supremum, observe its outcome, update the information state, debit its cost, and apply the recursion again. On stopping, return a terminal recommendation attaining \(g(D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use a Bellman recursion over the information state and remaining budget, comparing the optimal terminal recommendation value with the expected value of each affordable continuation.

children.title: Stopping-Recommendation Decision Coupling
children.top_down_role: Stopping and terminal recommendation treated as coupled decisions.

children.title: Budget-Exhaustion Termination
children.top_down_role: Termination imposed externally by a resource limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Budget-Exhaustion Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: External stopping condition induced solely by the remaining resource budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b_t\geq0\) be the remaining budget at stage \(t\), let \(A_t\) be the available evaluation actions, and let each action have cost \(c_t(a)>0\). The budget-exhaustion stopping time is
\[\tau_B=\inf\left\{t\geq0:\{a\in A_t:c_t(a)\leq b_t\}=\varnothing\right\}.\]
Before \(\tau_B\), a selected action \(a_t\) must satisfy \(c_t(a_t)\leq b_t\), and the budget updates as \(b_{t+1}=b_t-c_t(a_t)\). At \(\tau_B\), evaluation terminates and the current terminal recommendation rule is applied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop at the first stage when the remaining budget cannot pay for any available evaluation, then issue the current terminal recommendation.
assumptions_latex: Remaining budget is nonnegative and action costs are strictly positive.
No borrowing, partial action, or budget replenishment is permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\tau_B=\inf\left\{t\geq0:\min_{a\in A_t}c_t(a)>b_t\right\},\] with the convention that the minimum over an empty set is \(+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Available evaluation actions at stage t.

review_flags: The condition is standard but lacks a supplied source explicitly defining budget-exhaustion stopping.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stopping-time definition is coherent, equivalent to the displayed minimum-cost form under the stated empty-set convention, and condition is the correct content kind. No source or explicit standard-field rationale is supplied for the record.

children.title: Value-of-Continuation Termination
children.top_down_role: Adaptive stopping based on the value of further information.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-of-Continuation Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping by comparison of optimal continuation value with immediate terminal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At information state \(D_t\) with remaining budget \(b_t\), let \(g(D_t)\) be the value of stopping immediately. For each affordable action \(a\), define
\[Q_t(a)=\mathbb E_t\!\left[V(T(D_t,a,Y_a),b_t-c(a))\right].\]
The value-of-continuation stopping time is
\[\tau_V=\inf\left\{t\geq0:\sup_{a:c(a)\leq b_t}Q_t(a)\leq g(D_t)\right\}.\]
Thus evaluation continues only if some affordable action has strictly positive net continuation value relative to immediate stopping. At \(\tau_V\), apply the terminal recommendation attaining \(g(D_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop when no affordable action has expected downstream value exceeding the value of making the terminal recommendation immediately.
assumptions_latex: Continuation and terminal values are finite and expressed in the same utility units.
The conditional continuation values are measurable at each information state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sup_{a:c(a)\leq b_t}Q_t(a)\leq g(D_t)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{stop}.\]

notation.meaning: Expected value after taking action a and acting optimally thereafter.

source_refs.locator: 1.6.2 Policies based on lookahead approximations p. 20
2.9.3 Expected Value of Perfect Information p. 154

review_flags: The sources are provisional for the exact optimal-stopping formulation.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.6.2 Policies based on lookahead approximations p. 20
2.9.3 Expected Value of Perfect Information p. 154

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuation-versus-stopping condition is mathematically coherent and matches the leaf. The cited lookahead and expected-value-of-perfect-information sections do not, from the supplied evidence, specifically support this stopping-time formulation; full-text confirmation or a direct optimal-stopping source is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adaptive termination by value of continuation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-horizon Bayesian optimization model with an irreversible termination action, including compulsory termination at the observation limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A=\mathcal X\cup\{\varnothing\}\), where \(\varnothing\) is an absorbing termination action that adds no data, and assume a finite observation bound \(\tau_{\max}\). Then \(\alpha_\tau(\varnothing;\mathcal D)=0\). At any decision before compulsory termination, \(\varnothing\) is optimal if and only if \(\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\alpha_\tau(x;\mathcal D)\le 0\); at \(\tau_{\max}\), termination is compelled independently of this comparison. With utility measuring progress but not observation cost, the pre-limit stopping condition may be unattainable; incorporating observation costs can make it attainable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absorbing stop action has zero expected marginal gain because it adds no data and permits no later observation. Before the finite observation limit, stopping is optimal exactly when no observation has positive expected marginal utility. At the limit, stopping is mandatory regardless of continuation value. A progress-only utility may never favor early stopping, whereas including observation costs can permit it.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A=\mathcal X\cup\{\varnothing\}
\tau_{\max}<\infty
\varnothing\text{ is absorbing and adds no observations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha_\tau(\varnothing;\mathcal D)=0;\quad \tau<\tau_{\max}\implies\left(\varnothing\text{ is optimal}\iff\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\alpha_\tau(x;\mathcal D)\le 0\right),\quad \tau=\tau_{\max}\implies\varnothing\text{ is compulsory}.
