children.title: Feedback Latency Failures
children.top_down_role: Search degradation caused by decisions made without recent outcomes.

children.title: Delayed Outcome Feedback
children.top_down_role: Observation regimes with substantial lag between evaluation launch and outcome receipt.

knowledge_statements.title: Delayed Outcome Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observation model in which evaluation results arrive after random or deterministic lags.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For decisions issued at times \(t=1,2,\ldots\), let \(X_t\in\mathcal X\) be the evaluated input, \(Y_t\) its outcome, and \(\Delta_t\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}\) its feedback delay. Outcome \(Y_t\) becomes observable at time \(A_t=t+\Delta_t\). The information available immediately before decision \(n\) is
\[\mathcal F_{n^-}=\sigma\!\left(X_1,\ldots,X_{n-1},\{Y_t:A_t<n\},\{A_t<n\}:t<n\right).\]
A delayed-feedback policy requires \(X_n\) to be measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_{n^-}\), so unresolved outcomes cannot influence that decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each evaluation outcome arrives after a lag, and every new proposal may depend only on inputs and outcomes revealed before its decision time.
assumptions_latex: Decision and arrival times are indexed on a common discrete clock.
Each delay \(\Delta_t\) is nonnegative or infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_n\) must be \(\mathcal F_{n^-}\)-measurable, excluding unrevealed \(Y_t\) from the decision.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the sigma-field expression uses ambiguous random-set and event notation, especially the term describing arrival indicators. A precise delayed-feedback source is required to validate and normalize the information structure.

children.title: Stale Posterior Decisions
children.top_down_role: Search decisions based on a posterior lacking recent outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale Posterior Decisions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies decision loss from optimizing an outdated rather than current posterior acquisition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a_s,a_t:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be acquisition functions computed from information available at times \(s<t\). Let \(x_s\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X}a_s(x)\) and \(x_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X}a_t(x)\). If \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|a_t(x)-a_s(x)|\leq\varepsilon\), then the stale-decision loss under the current acquisition satisfies
\[0\leq a_t(x_t)-a_t(x_s)\leq2\varepsilon.\]
Without a bound on acquisition drift, choosing from the stale posterior admits no corresponding uniform decision-quality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If old and current acquisitions differ uniformly by at most epsilon, optimizing the old one loses at most twice epsilon under the current criterion; unbounded drift removes this guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Both acquisition functions attain maxima on \(\mathcal X\).
Their uniform difference is at most \(\varepsilon<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_t(x_t)-a_t(x_s)\leq2\varepsilon\); absent controlled drift, no uniform bound follows.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The 2-epsilon bound is mathematically correct and the failure-boundary kind fits, but no cited source establishes this as the intended stale-posterior result in the local Bayesian-optimization context.

children.title: Delay-Aware Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Evaluation policies that account for expected feedback latency.

knowledge_statements.title: Delay-Aware Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation criteria average performance over both objective uncertainty and feedback delays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a policy \(\pi\) issue evaluations over a horizon \(T\), and let \(A_i=i+\Delta_i\) be the arrival time of outcome \(Y_i\). For minimization, define the best observed value by time \(T\) as
\[B_T^\pi=\min\{Y_i:A_i\leq T\},\]
with \(B_T^\pi=+\infty\) if no outcome has arrived. A delay-aware performance criterion is \(R_T(\pi)=\mathbb E[B_T^\pi-f^*]\), where the expectation includes objective observations, policy randomization, and delays. Policies compared by \(R_T\) are charged for useful results arriving after the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assess a policy using only outcomes received by the deadline and average regret over observation noise, policy randomness, and feedback delays.
assumptions_latex: The objective has finite optimum value \(f^*\).
Arrival times satisfy \(A_i=i+\Delta_i\).
The expectation defining \(R_T(\pi)\) is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T(\pi)\) measures horizon regret using received, rather than merely launched, evaluations.

notation.meaning: best outcome received by horizon T

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the leaf, but assigning positive infinity when no outcome arrives can make the expected regret infinite and unsuitable for policy comparison unless that event has probability zero or a finite censoring convention is supplied. The proposed metric also lacks a direct source.

children.title: Feedback Obsolescence
children.top_down_role: Loss of decision relevance when outcomes arrive after substantial search progress.

assumptions_latex: Decisions occur at times \(t=1,2,\ldots\), and evaluation \(i\) returns after delay \(D_i\ge 0\).
The posterior or acquisition rule may change while an evaluation is pending.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feedback from evaluation \(i\) is obsolete at completion if \(a_{i+D_i}(x_i)\le \tau_{i+D_i}\), despite \(a_i(x_i)>\tau_i\) when dispatched.

notation.meaning: Acquisition value at decision time t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes obsolescence as loss of decision value between dispatch and delayed completion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-relative obsolescence of delayed Bayesian-optimization feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose evaluation \(i\) is dispatched at time \(i\) at candidate \(x_i\), returns at time \(i+D_i\), and satisfies \(a_i(x_i)>\tau_i\). Its feedback is obsolete relative to the completion-time decision rule when \[a_{i+D_i}(x_i)\le \tau_{i+D_i}.\] Thus obsolescence is not merely positive delay: it occurs when posterior updates, incumbent changes, or remaining-budget changes make the completed observation fail the current usefulness criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delayed feedback is obsolete when an evaluation valuable at dispatch no longer meets the decision rule's usefulness threshold when it finishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Feedback Obsolescence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the proposed usefulness-threshold convention is not canonical and has no cited source establishing this formulation.

children.title: Heterogeneous Worker Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Assignment of evaluations to resources with unequal speed, capability, or reliability.

children.title: Capability-Constrained Workers
children.top_down_role: Workers restricted to particular sources, tasks, or candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Capability-Constrained Workers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static eligibility constraints for heterogeneous evaluation workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\subseteq W\times J\times\mathcal X\) contain precisely the worker-task-candidate triples that can be executed. A binary assignment \(z\) is capability-feasible if and only if \[z_{wjx}=0\quad\text{for every }(w,j,x)\notin E.\] If each selected task-candidate pair must be assigned once and every worker has unit capacity, feasibility additionally requires \(\sum_{w\in W}z_{wjx}=1\) for each selected \((j,x)\) and \(\sum_{j,x}z_{wjx}\le 1\) for each \(w\in W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capability-feasible assignment never assigns a worker to an ineligible task-candidate pair. Assignment-once and worker-capacity constraints apply when those additional scheduling requirements are imposed.
assumptions_latex: There is a finite worker set \(W\), task set \(J\), and candidate domain \(\mathcal X\).
Worker eligibility is known before assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An assignment \(z\) is capability-feasible exactly when \(z_{wjx}=0\) for every \((w,j,x)\notin E\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: eligibility-set constraints are the standard mathematical encoding of heterogeneous worker capabilities
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Runtime-Aware Assignment
children.top_down_role: Scheduling incorporating predicted evaluation duration.

assumptions_latex: At a scheduling epoch, idle workers and admissible candidate-worker pairs are known.
For each admissible pair, a utility estimate and positive predicted runtime are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule returns a feasible assignment maximizing predicted utility per unit evaluation time, or another declared runtime-adjusted score.

notation.meaning: Predicted Bayesian-optimization utility of assigning x to w

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: utility-rate maximization is a standard runtime-aware scheduling rule
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Myopic utility-rate assignment with capability and capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At scheduling time \(t\), compute \(u_t(x,w)\) and \(r_t(x,w)>0\) for every admissible candidate-worker pair. Choose \[A_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{A\in\mathcal F_t}\sum_{(x,w)\in A}\frac{u_t(x,w)}{r_t(x,w)}.\] Dispatch all pairs in \(A_t\), update runtime and objective models when outcomes arrive, and repeat while budget remains and a worker is available. Stop when the resource budget is exhausted or no feasible positive-utility assignment exists; output the best observed feasible candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each scheduling epoch, assign eligible workers to candidates by maximizing predicted Bayesian-optimization utility per unit runtime under capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Runtime-Aware Assignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but maximizing a sum of pairwise utility/runtime ratios is one particular heuristic and is not generally identical to maximizing aggregate utility per aggregate time. A source must support this exact runtime-adjusted rule and its stopping convention.

children.title: Interruptible Evaluation Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Scheduling with interruptible or transferable evaluations.

children.title: Evaluation Preemption
children.top_down_role: Interruption of active evaluations to release resources.

assumptions_latex: A running evaluation has state \(s(t)\) and has consumed resource \(c(t)\) at time \(t\).
The scheduler observes a stopping signal and a declared rule for retaining or discarding partial state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Preemption stops the evaluation at a stopping time and releases its worker, with subsequent value determined by the retained-state convention.

notation.meaning: Evaluation state after elapsed time t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stopping-time semantics distinguish preemption from ordinary completion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduler-initiated interruption of a running evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a running evaluation, choose a stopping time \(\tau\) with respect to the scheduler's observed history. At \(\tau\), suspend execution, charge consumed resource \(c(\tau)\), release the worker, and apply the declared state rule: retain \(s(\tau)\) for resumption, convert it to an admissible partial observation, or discard it. If resumed, continue from the retained state; otherwise mark the evaluation terminated. The preemption rule is feasible only when these state and accounting operations are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation preemption interrupts a running job at a scheduler-chosen stopping time, releases its worker, and explicitly retains, reports, or discards partial state.
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation Preemption

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic treatment fits evaluation preemption, but no citation supports the stopping-time, partial-observation, state-retention, and accounting conventions used here.

children.title: Checkpoint-Based Migration
children.top_down_role: Transfer of preserved evaluation state between workers.

assumptions_latex: The evaluation admits serializable checkpoints at designated times.
A destination worker is compatible with the checkpoint and candidate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Migration preserves completed computational progress when restoration reproduces the checkpoint state, subject to explicit transfer and restart costs.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: checkpoint-restore semantics are standard for migratable computations
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-preserving migration between compatible heterogeneous workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At checkpoint time \(t_k\), serialize the evaluation state as \(s_k\), preempt the source worker, transfer \(s_k\) to a compatible destination \(w'\), and restore execution from \(s_k\). A migration is state-preserving when the restored process has the same continuation law as uninterrupted execution conditional on \(s_k\). Charge checkpoint, transfer, queueing, and restoration resources before resumption. Stop normally after completion, or return the latest valid checkpoint if migration cannot finish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Checkpoint-based migration serializes a running evaluation, transfers it to a compatible worker, and resumes with the same conditional continuation law.
knowledge_statements.title: Checkpoint-Based Migration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and checkpoint-restore sequence fit the container, but the claimed continuation-law equivalence and fallback behavior require a source with explicit migration semantics.

children.title: Migration Overhead
children.top_down_role: Communication, serialization, and restart costs associated with transfer.

assumptions_latex: An evaluation may be migrated from worker \(w\) to worker \(w'\) at checkpoint \(k\).
All time components are nonnegative and measured on a common scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Migration is latency-beneficial only if its overhead is smaller than the completion-time reduction obtained on the destination worker.

notation.meaning: Predicted remaining runtime on worker w
Checkpoint, transfer, queueing, and restore times

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: additive overhead accounting yields the direct break-even condition for migration
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Break-even condition for migrating a checkpointed evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the migration overhead by \[h_k(w,w')=c_k+d_k(w,w')+q_k(w')+r_k(w'),\] where the terms denote checkpoint creation, transfer, destination queueing, and restoration time. Relative to uninterrupted execution on \(w\), migration reduces predicted completion latency exactly when \[h_k(w,w')+R_k(w')<R_k(w).\] Equality is the latency break-even boundary; if the inequality is reversed, migration cannot be justified by completion time alone, although other resource or reliability objectives may still favor it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Migration is faster only when checkpointing, transfer, queueing, and restoration overhead is less than the destination worker's predicted runtime advantage.
knowledge_statements.title: Migration Overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The break-even inequality is correct under the declared additive model, and the condition role fits. No source establishes that model or clarifies whether destination runtime excludes the separately counted queueing and restoration terms.

children.title: Nontransferable Evaluation State
children.top_down_role: Evaluation regimes where active computation cannot move safely between workers.

assumptions_latex: A running evaluation has internal state \(s\) on source worker \(w\).
Continuation on destination worker \(w'\) requires an admissible encoding and restoration map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a valid state transfer, migration cannot preserve progress and must restart, remain on the source, or terminate.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: transferability requires a semantics-preserving encode-restore composition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of progress-preserving migration across incompatible workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The state \(s\) is transferable from \(w\) to \(w'\) only if an encoding \(E_w(s)\) is admissible at \(w'\) and restoration satisfies \[R_{w'}(E_w(s))\sim s,\] where \(\sim\) denotes equality of the conditional continuation law relevant to the evaluation output. If either map is undefined or the equivalence fails, the state is nontransferable. Consequently, preemption followed by placement on \(w'\) loses completed progress and requires restart, source-worker continuation, or termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation state is nontransferable when it cannot be encoded and restored on another worker while preserving the output's conditional continuation law.
knowledge_statements.title: Nontransferable Evaluation State

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the continuation-law equivalence is a chosen formalization of transferability and needs a source specifying the relevant state and platform semantics.

children.title: Incomplete Evaluation Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Incomplete or unusually slow evaluations treated as scheduling information.

children.title: Straggler Detection
children.top_down_role: Identification of evaluations exhibiting unusually slow progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Straggler Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predictive tail-probability test for unusually slow evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At time \(t\), for every unfinished evaluation \(i\), compute its conditional survival probability beyond a declared boundary \(b_i(t)>t\). Flag \(i\) as a straggler precisely when \[\Pr\!\left(T_i>b_i(t)\mid T_i>t,\mathcal H_t\right)\ge \alpha.\] The boundary may be a service-level deadline or a predictive runtime quantile, but it and \(\alpha\) must be fixed before classification. The flag alone does not imply failure or authorize treating the objective outcome as observed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A running evaluation is a straggler when its predicted conditional probability of missing a declared completion boundary is at least a fixed threshold.
assumptions_latex: For a running evaluation, a predictive distribution of completion time is available conditional on current information.
A tail-probability threshold \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A running evaluation is flagged as a straggler when its conditional probability of exceeding the declared deadline is at least \(\alpha\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: predictive tail threshold is a checkable model-based definition of a straggler
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Evaluation Failure
children.top_down_role: Evaluations that terminate without a usable objective outcome.

assumptions_latex: Each dispatched evaluation has a declared success event and terminal status.
A successful evaluation returns an admissible objective observation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure is the terminal event \(F_i=1\), distinct from an evaluation that is merely incomplete or slow.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: separates terminal failure from pending execution and defines observability explicitly
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal failure of an objective evaluation, excluding pending jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For dispatched evaluation \(i\), define \(F_i=1\) when execution terminates without producing an admissible objective observation \(Y_i\in\mathcal Y\), and define \(F_i=0\) when such an observation is returned. A job still running at the analysis time has neither terminal classification unless the protocol declares a timeout to be failure. Failure metadata may itself be observed, but it is not an objective value unless the statistical model explicitly defines a failure outcome or penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evaluation fails when it terminates without an admissible objective observation; a still-running or censored evaluation is not automatically a failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes terminal failure from pending or censored execution, but the precise admissibility and timeout conventions lack a supporting citation.

children.title: Runtime Censoring
children.top_down_role: Partial duration information from interrupted or unfinished evaluations.

assumptions_latex: Evaluation runtime \(T_i\ge 0\) is observed only until a censoring time \(C_i\ge 0\).
The censoring indicator is recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The runtime observation is \((U_i,\Delta_i)\), which gives an exact runtime only when \(\Delta_i=1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the standard right-censoring representation from survival analysis
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Right-censored runtimes for unfinished or administratively stopped evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_i\) be the true runtime and \(C_i\) the censoring time. The observed runtime record is \[U_i=\min\{T_i,C_i\},\qquad \Delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}.\] If \(\Delta_i=1\), then \(U_i=T_i\) is an exact completion time. If \(\Delta_i=0\), only \(T_i>U_i\) is known. Replacing a censored record by the equality \(T_i=U_i\) changes the likelihood and generally biases runtime estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime censoring records the minimum of completion and censoring times plus an indicator showing whether the observed time is exact or only a lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Runtime Censoring

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The right-censoring representation is mathematically standard and the definition role fits, but no authoritative survival-analysis source with an inspectable locator is cited.

children.title: Informative Missingness
children.top_down_role: Missing outcomes whose occurrence carries information about candidates or workers.

assumptions_latex: A latent objective outcome \(Y_i\) is associated with every attempted candidate \(X_i\).
The indicator \(M_i=1\) means the objective outcome is missing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Missingness is informative when its conditional law depends on the unobserved outcome after conditioning on recorded predictors.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conditional dependence on the unseen outcome is the standard nonignorable-missingness criterion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonignorable missing objective outcomes in asynchronous evaluation data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Missingness is informative relative to recorded predictors \((X_i,Z_i)\) when there exist outcome values \(y_1,y_2\) with positive conditional support such that \[\Pr(M_i=1\mid Y_i=y_1,X_i,Z_i)\ne\Pr(M_i=1\mid Y_i=y_2,X_i,Z_i).\] Equivalently, \(M_i\not\!\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_i\mid(X_i,Z_i)\). Consequently, a likelihood based only on observed \(Y_i\) values and treating missingness as ignorable need not identify the objective response model without additional assumptions or a joint missingness model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Missingness is informative when evaluation failure or nonreturn remains statistically dependent on the unseen objective value after conditioning on recorded information.
knowledge_statements.title: Informative Missingness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-dependence criterion fits informative missingness, but the nonignorability and identification conclusion requires an authoritative missing-data source and explicit regular-conditional-probability conventions.

children.title: Batch Acquisition Computation
children.top_down_role: Computational organization of high-dimensional batch policy evaluation and optimization.

children.title: Reparameterized Monte Carlo Batch Utilities
children.top_down_role: Sample-based evaluation and differentiation of joint batch utilities.

assumptions_latex: At batch \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_q)\), the posterior admits a differentiable reparameterization \(Y(X)=\mu(X)+L(X)\varepsilon\).
The utility \(u(Y;\mathcal D)\) is integrable, and pathwise differentiation is justified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The batch utility and its gradient are represented by expectations over parameter-free noise and estimated by common-noise Monte Carlo averages.

notation.meaning: Posterior factor satisfying LL transpose equals posterior covariance

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Gaussian reparameterization and pathwise Monte Carlo differentiation are standard for joint batch acquisitions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian pathwise representation for differentiable joint batch acquisitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For posterior batch outcomes \(Y(X)=\mu(X)+L(X)\varepsilon\), define \[A(X)=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon}\!\left[u\!\left(\mu(X)+L(X)\varepsilon;\mathcal D\right)\right].\] With independent draws \(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_M\), the reparameterized estimator is \[\widehat A_M(X)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M u\!\left(\mu(X)+L(X)\varepsilon_m;\mathcal D\right).\] When differentiation and expectation may be interchanged, \(\nabla_X A(X)=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon}[\nabla_X u(\mu(X)+L(X)\varepsilon;\mathcal D)]\), and differentiating \(\widehat A_M\) gives an unbiased pathwise gradient estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Express joint posterior outcomes using parameter-free noise, average sampled batch utilities, and differentiate through the samples when pathwise regularity permits.
knowledge_statements.title: Reparameterized Monte Carlo Batch Utilities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits and the Gaussian reparameterized estimator is standard. A batch-acquisition source is needed to support the interchange of differentiation and expectation and the resulting unbiased-gradient claim under adequate integrability and differentiability conditions.

children.title: Joint Batch Numerical Optimization
children.top_down_role: Continuous inner optimization over joint batch variables.

children.title: Batch Acquisition Gradients
children.top_down_role: Derivative information for continuous optimization of joint batch utilities.

assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is compact and \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_q)\in D^q\).
For almost every \(z\), \(u(\cdot,z)\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of \(D^q\).
There is an integrable \(M(z)\) such that \(\|\nabla_Xu(X,z)\|\le M(z)\) uniformly on that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[
abla_X\alpha_q(X)=\mathbb{E}[
abla_Xu(X,Z)],\qquad \widehat g_m(X)= rac1m\sum_{r=1}^m
abla_Xu(X,Z_r).\]

notation.meaning: Ordered batch of q candidate points
Reparameterized random variable independent of the batch

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pathwise gradient identity for a differentiable reparameterized batch acquisition.

source_refs.locator: 5. Parametric Optimization: Stochastic Gradients and Adaptive Search p. 71
source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\) be independent copies of \(Z\), and define the reparameterized batch acquisition by \(\alpha_q(X)=\mathbb{E}[u(X,Z)]\). Under the stated differentiability and domination assumptions, differentiation may be interchanged with expectation. Consequently, the sample-average pathwise gradient \(\widehat g_m(X)\) is unbiased for \(\nabla_X\alpha_q(X)\). Its block corresponding to \(x_i\) supplies the simultaneous search direction for the \(i\)-th member of the batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable reparameterized batch utility can be differentiated inside its expectation; averaging pathwise sample gradients gives an unbiased joint gradient estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Batch Acquisition Gradients

children.title: Joint Batch Numerical Search
children.top_down_role: Numerical optimization over coupled batch decision variables.

assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is compact and the batch size \(q\ge1\) is fixed.
The computable objective \(\widehat\alpha_q:D^q\to\mathbb{R}\) is a deterministic or common-random-number approximation of the batch acquisition.
A numerical local-search routine and a finite initialization set \(S\subset D^q\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat X\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{X\,\in\,\{L(z):z\in S\}}\widehat\alpha_q(X),\] where \(L(z)\) is the feasible terminal point returned from initialization \(z\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multistart numerical maximization over the full ordered batch.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(D\), \(q\), \(\widehat\alpha_q\), the initialization set \(S\), and a stopping tolerance \(\tau>0\). For every \(z\in S\), run constrained local maximization jointly in all \(qd\) coordinates, using batch gradients when available, until the projected step or acquisition improvement is at most \(\tau\); denote the feasible terminal point by \(L(z)\). Evaluate \(\widehat\alpha_q\) at all terminal points and return one attaining the largest value. Permutation-equivalent batches may be canonicalized before comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize all batch locations together from several starts, stop each local run at tolerance, and return the terminal batch with greatest computed acquisition.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Batch Numerical Search

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Cyclic optimization sequentially refines each member of a batch, cycling through the members until a good acquisition score is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cyclic optimization repeatedly cycles through a batch and sequentially refines each member until a good acquisition score is reached.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{This cyclic sequential-refinement procedure is called cyclic optimization.}

children.title: Initialization Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of batch solutions on numerical starting configurations.

assumptions_latex: \(D^q\) has a reference probability measure \(\mu\), and \(L:D^q\to D^q\) is a deterministic local-search terminal map.
The acquisition \(\alpha_q:D^q\to\mathbb{R}\) has two terminal points \(X_a=L(z_a)\) and \(X_b=L(z_b)\) with unequal values.
Their attraction basins \(B_a=L^{-1}(X_a)\) and \(B_b=L^{-1}(X_b)\) have positive \(\mu\)-measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathbb{P}\!\left(\alpha_q(L(Z))=\alpha_q(X_a)\right)\ge\mu(B_a)>0,\qquad Z\sim\mu,\] so the returned acquisition value depends nontrivially on initialization.

notation.meaning: Terminal point produced by local search from a start
Attraction basin of terminal point X_i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of local batch optimization on attraction basins.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a random initialization \(Z\sim\mu\), the probability of terminating at \(X_i\) equals \(\mu(B_i)\). Hence, if two positive-measure basins lead to terminal points with different acquisition values, the local optimizer's output and achieved value are nonconstant functions of its initialization. With \(r\) independent starts, the probability of missing a designated basin \(B_i\) is \((1-\mu(B_i))^r\), which decreases with restart count but remains positive for finite \(r\) whenever \(0<\mu(B_i)<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct positive-measure attraction basins make the optimized batch depend on its start; multiple independent restarts reduce, but do not eliminate, basin-missing risk.
knowledge_statements.title: Initialization Sensitivity

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

children.title: Local-Optimum Failure
children.top_down_role: Batch-quality loss caused by suboptimal inner numerical solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Optimum Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete smooth acquisition with a strictly suboptimal local maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\delta<8/(3\sqrt{3})\), the smooth acquisition \(\alpha(x)=-(x^2-1)^2+\delta x\) on \([-2,2]\) has two strict local maximizers \(x_-<0<x_+\) with \(\alpha(x_-)<\alpha(x_+)\). A local-ascent method initialized in the attraction basin of \(x_-\) may terminate at \(x_-\), so stationarity of the returned point does not certify global acquisition optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tilted double-well acquisition has two strict local maxima of unequal height, so local ascent from the left basin can return the inferior peak and fail to find the global optimum.
assumptions_latex: The local-ascent method converges to the local maximizer associated with its initialization's attraction basin.
The stopping rule may accept a stationary local maximizer without comparing it globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists\,x_-<0<x_+\text{ such that both are strict local maximizers and }\alpha(x_-)<\alpha(x_+);\] every initialization in the attraction basin of \(x_-\) may therefore return a strictly suboptimal acquisition value.

notation.meaning: Positive tilt parameter separating the peak values
Left and right strict local maximizers

children.title: Distributed Batch Approximations
children.top_down_role: Decomposed acquisition computations for large batches or multiple agents.

assumptions_latex: The batch index set \(I=\{1,ldots,q\}\) is partitioned into nonempty blocks \(I_1,ldots,I_K\).
Each agent \(k\) can evaluate a local surrogate acquisition \(a_k(X_{I_k};c_k)\), where \(c_k\) summarizes communicated beliefs about other blocks.
A deterministic aggregation rule \(A\) and communication-update rule \(C\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widetilde\alpha_q(X)=A\!\left(a_1(X_{I_1};c_1),\ldots,a_K(X_{I_K};c_K)\right)\] is the distributed approximation, with messages updated by \((c_1,ldots,c_K)\leftarrow C(X,c_1,ldots,c_K)\).

notation.meaning: Partition block assigned to agent k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract decomposition of a joint acquisition across batch blocks or agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A distributed batch approximation consists of a partition \(I_1,ldots,I_K\), local acquisition maps \(a_k\), finite messages \(c_k\), an aggregation rule \(A\), and a communication rule \(C\). Given current messages, agents optimize their block variables in parallel or asynchronously. The resulting block proposals are combined into \(X\), messages are refreshed through \(C\), and the process stops at a prescribed iteration or message-residual tolerance. The construction is exact only when the chosen aggregation and messages preserve every cross-block dependence of the original \(\alpha_q\); otherwise \(\widetilde\alpha_q\) is an approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition the batch among agents, optimize local acquisition contributions using exchanged summaries, aggregate the contributions, and recognize omitted cross-block dependence as approximation error.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Batch Approximations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this particular distributed-acquisition formalization, its aggregation semantics, or its exactness claim. The arbitrary maps A and C do not by themselves characterize a recognized approximation method. Several occurrences of ldots also lack the required LaTeX command prefix.

children.title: High-Dimensional Multi-Fidelity Search
children.top_down_role: Dimension reduction and source selection coupled in a common search problem.

children.title: Shared Latent Structure Across Fidelities
children.top_down_role: Dimension-reducing structure transferred between sources.

assumptions_latex: The design domain is \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), fidelities belong to a finite set \(S\), and latent dimension \(r<d\).
The matrix \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\) has orthonormal columns and is common to all fidelities.
For each \(s\in S\), \(g_s:\mathbb{R}^r\to\mathbb{R}\) and discrepancy \(\varepsilon_s:D\to\mathbb{R}\) are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f_s(x)=g_s(W^{\mathsf T}x)+\varepsilon_s(x),\qquad x\in D,quad s\in S.\]

notation.meaning: Residual not explained by shared structure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common linear active subspace with fidelity-specific latent responses and residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Shared latent structure across fidelities is represented by a single projection \(W^{\mathsf T}x\) through which every fidelity response primarily varies. Fidelity dependence is retained in the latent functions \(g_s\), while \(\varepsilon_s\) records variation outside the shared subspace. The exact shared-subspace model is the special case \(\varepsilon_s\equiv0\) for every \(s\in S\). Thus observations at any fidelity can inform the common projection, whereas their response levels and shapes may remain fidelity-specific.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All fidelities depend primarily on one low-dimensional projection, while their latent response functions and residual discrepancies may differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared Latent Structure Across Fidelities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf, but no evidence establishes this shared active-subspace model as the intended multi-fidelity construction or supports the transfer claim. The conclusion also contains malformed D,quad s notation.

children.title: Fidelity-Dependent Active Structure
children.top_down_role: Relevant coordinates, interactions, or subspaces changing with fidelity.

assumptions_latex: The design domain is \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), fidelities belong to a finite set \(S\), and \(1\le r_sle d\).
For each \(s\in S\), \(W_s\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r_s}\) has orthonormal columns.
For each \(s\in S\), a latent response \(g_s:\mathbb{R}^{r_s}\to\mathbb{R}\) and residual \(\varepsilon_s:D\to\mathbb{R}\) are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f_s(x)=g_s(W_s^{\mathsf T}x)+\varepsilon_s(x),\qquad x\in D,quad s\in S,\] with no requirement that \(r_s=r_t\) or \(\operatorname{span}(W_s)=\operatorname{span}(W_t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fidelity-indexed active subspaces allowing changing dimensions and directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fidelity-dependent active structure permits each fidelity \(s\) to have its own active dimension and projection. Coordinates or directions outside \(\operatorname{span}(W_s)\) affect \(f_s\) only through the residual \(\varepsilon_s\). The structure changes between fidelities \(s\) and \(t\) whenever their active dimensions differ or their projection subspaces are unequal. A shared latent structure is recovered only under the additional restriction that a common matrix \(W\) can replace every \(W_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each fidelity may use a different active dimension or subspace; shared structure is the restricted case in which all projections coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Fidelity-Dependent Active Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fidelity-indexed subspace representation is plausible and locally relevant, but the selected model variant has no cited evidence. The assumptions contain malformed r_sle d notation and the conclusion contains malformed D,quad s notation.

children.title: Safe Constrained Multi-Fidelity Search
children.top_down_role: Objectives and feasibility information available through unequal-cost sources.

children.title: Constraint-Specific Fidelities
children.top_down_role: Separate fidelity structures for objective and constraint channels.

assumptions_latex: The objective channel is \(f_0:D\to\mathbb{R}\), and constraint channels are \(f_j:D\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(j=1,ldots,m\).
Each channel \(j\) has its own fidelity set \(S_j\), cost \(c_j:S_j\to(0,infty)\), and observation model \(Y_j(x,s)\).
Each \(S_j\) contains a designated target fidelity \(s_j^\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Y_j(x,s)=f_{j,s}(x)+\eta_{j,s},\qquad f_{j,s_j^\star}(x)=f_j(x),\qquad (j,s)\in\{0,ldots,m\}\times S_j.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate fidelity spaces and costs for objective and constraint observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Constraint-specific fidelities assign a distinct approximation family and resource scale to each objective or constraint channel. A permissible query is a triple \((x,j,s)\) with \(x\in D\) and \(s\in S_j\); it reveals only channel \(j\) through \(Y_j(x,s)\) and incurs cost \(c_j(s)\). Feasibility of a design is defined at target fidelities by \(f_j(x)\le0\) for every constraint \(j=1,ldots,m\). No common ordering or one-to-one correspondence among the sets \(S_j\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each objective or constraint has its own fidelity set, approximation family, target fidelity, observation noise, and query cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Specific Fidelities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation matches constraint-specific fidelities, but no source supports the channel-wise fidelity sets, target-fidelity convention, or observation model. Multiple commands are malformed, including ldots and infty.

children.title: Safe Fidelity Escalation
children.top_down_role: Progression toward expensive evaluations while managing feasibility risk.

assumptions_latex: Fidelities \(s_1\prec\cdots\prec s_L=s^\star\) have nondecreasing costs, and each constraint has posterior mean \(\mu_{j,\ell}(x)\) and deviation \(\sigma_{j,\ell}(x)\).
A confidence multiplier \(\beta>0\), escalation thresholds \(\tau_1,ldots,tau_{L-1}\), and a candidate \(x\in D\) are given.
Safety is interpreted through simultaneous upper confidence bounds for constraints \(f_j(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Escalation from \(s_\ell\) to \(s_{\ell+1}\) occurs only if \(U_{j,\ell}(x)le0\) for all \(j\) and \(\max_j\sigma_{j,\ell}(x)le\tau_\ell\); otherwise the algorithm rejects \(x\) or gathers more information without escalating it.

notation.meaning: Upper confidence bound for constraint j at fidelity level l

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Confidence-bound rule for advancing a candidate toward target fidelity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(U_{j,\ell}(x)=\mu_{j,\ell}(x)+\beta\sigma_{j,\ell}(x)\). Initialize at \(s_1\). After observing the candidate at level \(\ell\), update all constraint posteriors. If every \(U_{j,\ell}(x)\le0\) and the largest posterior deviation is at most \(\tau_\ell\), query \(x\) at \(s_{\ell+1}\); otherwise reject the candidate or select an additional information-gathering query. Stop upon rejection or after evaluating \(s^\star\), and declare target-fidelity safety only when all target-level upper bounds are nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Advance a candidate to a costlier fidelity only after all constraint upper bounds certify safety and uncertainty falls below the level's escalation threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Safe Fidelity Escalation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Safe Fidelity Escalation, but without a source and calibrated simultaneous confidence event, its upper-bound checks do not establish a safety guarantee. The assumptions and conclusion also contain malformed ldots, tau, and le commands.

children.title: Multiobjective Search with Partial Information
children.top_down_role: Pareto search with decoupled objectives, preferences, unequal costs, or distinct fidelities.

children.title: Decoupled Objective Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Selection of which objective to observe at each candidate.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\ge2\) objective functions \(f_1,ldots,f_m\) on \(D\), but a query may reveal only one objective.
The posterior state is \(\mathcal{D}\), and observing objective \(j\) at \(x\) costs \(c_j(x)>0\).
A terminal decision utility \(V(\mathcal{D})\) and observation model for each \((x,j)\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(x^\star,j^\star)\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in D,j\in\{1,ldots,m\}}\frac{\mathbb{E}[V(\mathcal{D}\cup\{(x,j,Y_j)\})\mid\mathcal{D}]-V(\mathcal{D})}{c_j(x)}.\]

notation.meaning: Cost of observing objective j at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step value-per-cost scheduling of a location and objective channel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each scheduling step, compute for every permissible pair \((x,j)\) the posterior expected increase in terminal utility produced by observing \(Y_j\) at \(x\), divided by its cost. Select a maximizing pair, observe only objective \(j^\star\) at \(x^\star\), update \(\mathcal{D}\), and repeat until the remaining budget is smaller than every available query cost or a prescribed value threshold is met. The rule permits different objectives to be measured at different designs and frequencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the design and objective channel with greatest expected terminal-utility gain per cost, observe that channel alone, update, and repeat within budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Decoupled Objective Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is a plausible one-step value-per-cost scheduler and fits the leaf, but no source supports this particular utility ratio or stopping rule. The objective-index notation contains malformed ldots commands.

children.title: Multi-Fidelity Pareto Search
children.top_down_role: Pareto discovery using source-dependent outcome accuracy.

assumptions_latex: The target objective vector is \(F(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x))\) on \(D\), with componentwise minimization.
Each fidelity \(s\in S\) supplies a posterior-coupled approximation \(F_s(x)\), has cost \(c(s)>0\), and includes a target fidelity \(s^\star\).
A posterior acquisition \(a(x,s;\mathcal{D})\) measures expected improvement in target-fidelity Pareto information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(x_t,s_t)\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{(x,s)\in D\times S}\frac{a(x,s;\mathcal{D}_t)}{c(s)},\qquad \widehat P_T=\operatorname{ND}\{\mathbb{E}[F_{s^\star}(x)\mid\mathcal{D}_T]:x\in C_T\}.\]

notation.meaning: Set of evaluated or retained candidate designs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-aware querying for target-fidelity Pareto-set estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a joint posterior over all objective-fidelity pairs and a candidate set \(C_0\). At iteration \(t\), select \((x_t,s_t)\) maximizing target-Pareto information value per cost, observe the available objective vector at that fidelity, update the posterior, and add \(x_t\) to \(C_t\). Stop when the budget is exhausted or all acquisition ratios fall below a threshold. Return the nondominated target-fidelity posterior predictions over \(C_T\); lower-fidelity nondominance alone does not establish membership in \(\widehat P_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Query the design and fidelity with greatest target-Pareto information value per cost, then return nondominated target-fidelity predictions rather than low-fidelity nondominated points.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Fidelity Pareto Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm belongs in Multi-Fidelity Pareto Search, but the unspecified acquisition a could represent materially different methods and guarantees. No citation supports the selection rule or the proposed posterior-mean nondominated return set.

children.title: Mixed-Feedback Query Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Allocation between expensive outcome evaluations and decision-maker feedback.

children.title: Outcome-Query Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Allocation of resources to objective or outcome measurements.

assumptions_latex: Outcome channels are indexed by \(J=\{1,ldots,m\}\), and query \((x,j)\) reveals \(Y_j(x)\) only.
The current information state is \(\mathcal{D}\), each query costs \(c_j(x)>0\), and remaining budget is \(B\).
A common terminal utility \(V\) makes values of different outcome queries comparable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(x^star,j^star)\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in D,j\in J:c_j(x)\le B}\frac{\mathbb{E}[V(\mathcal{D}\cup\{(x,j,Y_j(x))\})\mid\mathcal{D}]-V(\mathcal{D})}{c_j(x)}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget-feasible scheduling among heterogeneous outcome observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each budget-feasible outcome query \((x,j)\), integrate its possible observation under the current posterior and compute the resulting expected terminal-utility gain per unit cost. Execute a maximizing query, append its realized outcome to \(\mathcal{D}\), reduce \(B\) by \(c_j(x)\), and update all statistically coupled channels. Stop when no query is affordable or the maximum expected gain is nonpositive. The shared utility scale is essential: channel-specific scores cannot be ranked without a specified cross-channel calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank affordable design-outcome queries by expected common-utility gain per cost, execute the best query, update coupled beliefs and budget, and stop when none is worthwhile.
knowledge_statements.title: Outcome-Query Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Outcome-Query Scheduling, but no source supports its myopic common-utility-per-cost rule or stopping criterion. The assumptions contain malformed ldots notation, and the conclusion uses x^star and j^star instead of valid superscript-star commands.

children.title: Preference-Query Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Allocation of resources to decision-maker preference feedback.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D_n\) induces a posterior over an unknown vector outcome function \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^m\) and latent decision-maker utility \(u:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\).
Each admissible comparison \(q=(y,y')\in\mathcal Q_n\) has positive cost \(c_P(q)\) and a specified probabilistic response model.
The scheduling criterion \(V_P(q\mid\mathcal D_n)\) is the expected one-step increase of a fixed terminal decision value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_{n+1}\) is a cost-normalized Bayes-optimal preference query among the currently admissible comparisons.

notation.meaning: data available before scheduling query n+1
expected terminal-value gain from a preference query

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: one-step value-of-information scheduling with query cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step scheduling of pairwise preference feedback under a fixed posterior and terminal utility criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\mathcal D_n\), construct the admissible set \(\mathcal Q_n\). For every \(q\in\mathcal Q_n\), average over its posterior predictive response \(R_q\) and compute \[V_P(q\mid\mathcal D_n)=\mathbb E\!\left[J(\mathcal D_n\cup\{(q,R_q)\})-J(\mathcal D_n)\mid\mathcal D_n\right],\] where \(J\) is the prescribed terminal decision value. Schedule \[q_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{q\in\mathcal Q_n}\frac{V_P(q\mid\mathcal D_n)}{c_P(q)}.\] If \(\mathcal Q_n=\varnothing\), or if the maximum gain is nonpositive, issue no preference query; otherwise observe the response and append it to \(\mathcal D_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate each available preference comparison by its expected improvement in terminal decision value per unit cost, then issue a maximizing comparison unless none has positive value.
knowledge_statements.title: Preference-Query Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Preference-Query Scheduling and is internally coherent as a one-step, cost-normalized value-of-information rule, but no citation supports the particular terminal-value formulation, stopping rule, or Bayes-optimal characterization.

children.title: Cross-Query Value Comparison
children.top_down_role: Comparison of expected decision value across outcome and preference channels.

assumptions_latex: A common terminal functional \(J\) evaluates posterior states produced by every query type.
Each admissible query \(q\) has cost \(c(q)>0\), duration \(\tau(q)>0\), and a posterior predictive response law.
All candidate gains are conditioned on the same current information \(\mathcal D_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized quantities \(V(q\mid\mathcal D_n)/r(q)\) place heterogeneous query types on a common one-step decision-value scale.

notation.meaning: expected value of information of query q
chosen positive resource charge, such as cost or duration

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: heterogeneous queries are comparable through a shared terminal value and resource normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step comparison of outcome, constraint, and preference queries through a shared terminal objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every admissible query \(q\), define \[V(q\mid\mathcal D_n)=\mathbb E\!\left[J(\mathcal D_n\cup\{(q,R_q)\})-J(\mathcal D_n)\mid\mathcal D_n\right].\] Choose one resource convention before comparison, for example \(r(q)=c(q)\) for expenditure-limited search or \(r(q)=\tau(q)\) for sequential wall-clock search. Queries of different types are compared by \(V(q\mid\mathcal D_n)/r(q)\), provided their response laws and posterior updates are integrated under the same model. Raw acquisition values from distinct scales are not directly comparable unless they represent the same \(J\) and resource convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different feedback queries are comparable only after expressing their expected gains through one terminal objective and normalizing them by the same resource convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Query Value Comparison

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits Cross-Query Value Comparison, but the claim that heterogeneous queries become comparable through a shared terminal functional and a single resource normalization requires an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Decision-Maker Availability
children.top_down_role: Preference-query opportunities limited by access to human decision makers.

assumptions_latex: At decision epoch \(n\), the availability indicator \(A_n\in\{0,1\}\) is observed before a query is chosen.
Outcome-query and preference-query sets are \(\mathcal Q_n^O\) and \(\mathcal Q_n^P\), respectively.
Unavailable preference queries cannot be deferred without changing the modeled state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible action set is \(\mathcal Q_n^O\cup\mathcal Q_n^P\) when \(A_n=1\), and \(\mathcal Q_n^O\) when \(A_n=0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: availability acts as a state-dependent feasibility constraint on preference queries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observed binary availability as a feasibility constraint in mixed-feedback scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the epoch-dependent feasible query set by \[\mathcal Q_n(A_n)=\mathcal Q_n^O\cup\bigl(A_n\mathcal Q_n^P\bigr),\] with the convention \(1\mathcal Q_n^P=\mathcal Q_n^P\) and \(0\mathcal Q_n^P=\varnothing\). A scheduling policy \(\pi\) respects decision-maker availability precisely when \[\mathbb P_\pi\!\left(Q_n\in\mathcal Q_n(A_n)\right)=1\] at every decision epoch. Thus a preference query is feasible only when \(A_n=1\); when \(A_n=0\), the policy must select an outcome query or stop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid policy may request preferences only at epochs when the decision maker is available; otherwise it must choose an outcome query or stop.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Maker Availability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition matches the availability leaf and consistently models observed binary availability as a feasibility constraint. No source supports this exact state-dependent action-set formulation or the assumption that unavailable queries cannot be deferred.

children.title: Parallel Constrained Pareto Search
children.top_down_role: Joint treatment of batch evaluation, feasibility, and multiple objectives.

assumptions_latex: The design domain is \(\mathcal X\), objectives are \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^m\), and feasibility means \(g_j(x)\le 0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\).
A posterior predictive model is available for all objectives and constraints after data \(\mathcal D_n\).
A batch contains \(B\ge 1\) distinct or repeatable design evaluations with a specified joint predictive law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected batch maximizes expected feasible hypervolume improvement and returns a posterior estimate of the feasible Pareto set after observation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: constrained batch Pareto search via expected feasible hypervolume improvement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous batch selection using expected feasible hypervolume improvement under joint posterior dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a reference point \(r\) dominated by all objective vectors of interest, and let \(P_n\) be the current feasible nondominated set for a maximization convention. For each candidate batch \(X_{1:B}\in\mathcal X^B\), draw jointly from the posterior of its objectives and constraints and define \[\alpha_n(X_{1:B})=\mathbb E\!\left[\operatorname{HV}_r\!\left(P_n\cup\{f(x_b):g(x_b)\le0\}_{b=1}^B\right)-\operatorname{HV}_r(P_n)\mid\mathcal D_n\right].\] Select a maximizing batch, evaluate every selected design, update the posterior, and stop at the prescribed batch or resource budget. The output is the posterior feasible nondominated set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a batch maximizing expected growth of feasible dominated hypervolume under the joint predictive model, evaluate it, and update the estimated feasible Pareto set.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Constrained Pareto Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Parallel Constrained Pareto Search, but the exact batch expected feasible hypervolume-improvement formula, joint feasibility treatment, and claimed output require a source specific to constrained batch multiobjective Bayesian optimization.

children.title: Multitask Resource Transfer
children.top_down_role: Allocation of observations across related tasks with unequal target value.

children.title: Auxiliary-Task Selection
children.top_down_role: Choosing which related task receives the next evaluation.

assumptions_latex: Tasks are indexed by \(t\in\{0,1,\ldots,T\}\), with target task \(t=0\), and share a joint posterior model.
Querying task \(t\) at \(x\in\mathcal X\) costs \(c_t(x)>0\).
The target terminal value is a functional \(J_0(\mathcal D)\) of the posterior for task \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The next auxiliary evaluation maximizes expected target-task value gained per unit task-specific cost.

notation.meaning: predictive observation for task t at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step selection among target and auxiliary tasks under a joint probabilistic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every admissible pair \((x,t)\in\mathcal X\times\{0,\\ldots,T\}\), compute the target-directed value of information \[V_t(x\mid\mathcal D_n)=\mathbb E\!\left[J_0\!\left(\mathcal D_n\cup\{(x,t,Y_t(x))\}\right)-J_0(\mathcal D_n)\mid\mathcal D_n\right].\] Select \[(x_{n+1},t_{n+1})\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{(x,t)}\frac{V_t(x\mid\mathcal D_n)}{c_t(x)}.\] Observe \(Y_{t_{n+1}}(x_{n+1})\), update the joint posterior, and repeat until the resource budget is exhausted or the maximal ratio is nonpositive. The selected task may be auxiliary, but its value is measured only through improvement of the target posterior decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the task and design whose observation yields the largest expected improvement in the target decision per unit cost, then update the shared model.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Task Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A source is required for this cost-sensitive multitask value-of-information algorithm. In addition, the task-index set contains the malformed command \\ldots, and the optimization includes target task t=0 even though the title and conclusion describe selection of an auxiliary task.

children.title: Cost-Transfer Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Balancing observation cost against expected target-task benefit.

children.title: Task-Specific Observation Cost
children.top_down_role: Unequal expenditure required to observe different auxiliary tasks.

assumptions_latex: Tasks are indexed by \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\) and designs by \(x\in\mathcal X\).
Each observation has a nonnegative monetary, temporal, or resource charge known when the query is scheduled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accumulated observation expenditure is the sum of the realized task-design costs and must not exceed the prescribed budget.

notation.meaning: cost of observing task t at design x

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive accounting for heterogeneous observation costs across tasks and designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A task-specific observation cost is a function \[c:\mathcal X\times\{0,\ldots,T\}\to[0,\infty),\qquad c(x,t)=c_t(x),\] whose value is the resource consumed by obtaining one observation of task \(t\) at design \(x\). For a scheduled sequence \((x_i,t_i)_{i=1}^n\), the cumulative observation cost is \[C_n=\sum_{i=1}^n c_{t_i}(x_i).\] Under a hard budget \(C\), the schedule is resource-feasible exactly when \(C_n\le C\). If costs are random but revealed only after execution, resource feasibility must instead be specified almost surely, in expectation, or by a chance constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each task-design observation consumes a specified resource amount; a schedule is feasible when the sum of its realized observation costs satisfies the chosen budget convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Task-Specific Observation Cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Task-Specific Observation Cost, but no source is cited. The record also blends costs known at scheduling time with costs revealed after execution, so an authoritative source is needed to select and state the intended deterministic or random-cost convention.

children.title: Target-Transfer Benefit
children.top_down_role: Expected target-task value obtained from auxiliary observations.

assumptions_latex: A joint posterior couples target task \(0\) with auxiliary task \(t\).
A fixed target terminal functional \(J_0\) is evaluated before and after a prospective auxiliary observation.
The prospective response \(Y_t(x)\) follows its current posterior predictive law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_t(x\mid\mathcal D)\) measures the expected target-only decision improvement attributable to observing auxiliary task \(t\) at \(x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: target-directed expected value of information defines transfer benefit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step expected benefit transferred from an auxiliary observation to the target decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The target-transfer benefit of querying auxiliary task \(t\ne0\) at design \(x\) is \[B_t(x\mid\mathcal D)=\mathbb E\!\left[J_0\!\left(\mathcal D\cup\{(x,t,Y_t(x))\}\right)-J_0(\mathcal D)\mid\mathcal D\right].\] The expectation integrates the auxiliary predictive response and the resulting joint-posterior update. This quantity records only improvement in the target-task terminal value; improvement confined to the auxiliary task does not count. Under a coherent decision-value functional and exact Bayesian updating, the option to ignore information implies \(B_t(x\mid\mathcal D)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Target-transfer benefit is the expected increase in a fixed target-task decision value after observing an auxiliary task and updating the joint posterior.
knowledge_statements.title: Target-Transfer Benefit

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches Target-Transfer Benefit, but the exact expected decision-value formulation and the nonnegativity claim depend on a formally specified coherent terminal decision problem and require authoritative support.

children.title: Cost–Transfer Tradeoff Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Efficient task choices across observation expense and target benefit.

assumptions_latex: The admissible query set is \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal X\times\{0,\ldots,T\}\).
Every query \(a\in\mathcal A\) has cost \(c(a)\ge0\) and target-transfer benefit \(B(a)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The frontier consists exactly of queries not weakly dominated in both cost and target-transfer benefit.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Pareto frontier under cost minimization and transfer-benefit maximization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto efficiency for minimizing query cost while maximizing target-transfer benefit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,a'\in\mathcal A\), say that \(a'\) cost-transfer dominates \(a\) when \(c(a')\le c(a)\) and \(B(a')\ge B(a)\), with at least one strict inequality. The cost-transfer tradeoff frontier is \[\mathcal F=\left\{(c(a),B(a)):a\in\mathcal A,\ \nexists a'\in\mathcal A\text{ that dominates }a\right\}.\] Equivalently, a query lies on the frontier precisely when no admissible query offers at least as much expected target benefit at no greater cost, with a strict improvement in one criterion. Scalar ratios such as \(B(a)/c(a)\) select supported preferences but do not define the entire frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cost-transfer frontier contains queries for which no alternative is both no more costly and at least as beneficial to the target, with one strict improvement.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost–Transfer Tradeoff Frontiers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto-frontier definition fits the leaf and correctly uses cost minimization with benefit maximization. A source is still required, especially for the additional claim about which preferences the ratio B(a)/c(a) selects.

children.title: Negative Transfer Risk
children.top_down_role: Target degradation caused by misleading auxiliary-task information.

assumptions_latex: A transfer policy \(\pi\) uses target and auxiliary observations, while a baseline policy \(\pi_0\) does not use auxiliary transfer.
Both policies are evaluated under the same data-generating distribution and resource budget \(C\).
Loss \(L(\pi;C)\) is measured on the target task only.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Negative transfer occurs when the transfer policy has strictly larger expected target loss than the no-transfer baseline.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: negative transfer is performance degradation relative to a matched no-transfer baseline
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational failure boundary relative to an equal-budget target-only baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the transfer effect at budget \(C\) by \[\Delta_C=\mathbb E[L(\pi;C)]-\mathbb E[L(\pi_0;C)].\] Negative transfer occurs exactly when \(\Delta_C>0\). Its risk at tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), under posterior uncertainty about task relatedness or model parameters, is \[R^-_C(\varepsilon)=\mathbb P\!\left(\mathbb E[L(\pi;C)-L(\pi_0;C)\mid\Theta]>\varepsilon\mid\mathcal D\right).\] The comparison is meaningful only when both policies share the target loss, budget, stopping rule, and evaluation distribution; otherwise degradation may reflect unequal resources rather than harmful transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transfer is harmful when, under matched resources and evaluation conditions, it raises expected target loss above a target-only baseline; posterior uncertainty yields a probability of such degradation.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative Transfer Risk

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is appropriate and the matched-baseline definition of negative transfer is plausible. The conditional posterior risk formula is a specific construction rather than a universal definition and needs an inspectable source.

children.title: Task–Source Identifiability
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity between task variation, fidelity bias, and observation noise.

assumptions_latex: Observations satisfy \(Y_i=f_{t_i}(x_i)+b_{s_i}(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), with task \(t_i\), source \(s_i\), and centered noise \(\varepsilon_i\).
The design has positive probability of sampling the task-source combinations invoked by the model.
An identifying constraint fixes the additive invariance, for example \(b_{s_0}(x)=0\) for a reference source \(s_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Task and source effects are identifiable exactly when equality of induced observation laws implies equality of their constrained parameterization.

notation.meaning: observation law indexed by model parameters

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: statistical identifiability is injectivity of the constrained parameter-to-law map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability in an additive task, source-bias, and noise decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta=(\{f_t\},\{b_s\},\eta)\), where \(\eta\) parameterizes the noise law, and impose the stated reference-source constraint. The task-source decomposition is identifiable on a parameter class \(\Theta\) when \[P_\theta=P_{\theta'}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\theta=\theta'\qquad\text{for all }\theta,\theta'\in\Theta.\] Without an identifying constraint, any function \(h:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) generates the observationally equivalent transformation \(f_t'=f_t+h\) and \(b_s'=b_s-h\). Moreover, unsampled task-source combinations or an unrestricted heteroscedastic noise law can preserve ambiguity; identifiability therefore requires both parameter restrictions and adequate incidence of tasks with sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Task effects, source bias, and noise are identifiable when the constrained model maps uniquely to observation laws; reference constraints and sufficient task-source overlap remove basic ambiguities.
knowledge_statements.title: Task–Source Identifiability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits Task–Source Identifiability, and injectivity of the parameter-to-law map is the correct general criterion. However, the record does not give sufficient precise restrictions on the function classes, noise family, and task-source incidence to substantiate identifiability for the stated additive model; a model-specific source is required.

children.title: Expensive Workflow Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Reusable interfaces connecting structured resource-aware Bayesian optimization to expensive workflows.

children.title: Multi-Fidelity Engineering Design
children.top_down_role: Coupling simulations, reduced models, and physical evaluations.

assumptions_latex: The physical response is \(f_H:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), and sources \(f_s\) have known costs \(c_s(x)>0\).
A joint surrogate specifies dependence between reduced models, simulations, and physical evaluations.
The final recommendation is judged using the high-fidelity physical response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multi-fidelity design selects design-source pairs by their expected high-fidelity decision gain per resource cost and returns a high-fidelity recommendation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: engineering fidelities represented by a shared physical response plus correlated source discrepancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint surrogate representation and resource-aware querying of engineering information sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent each information source by \[f_s(x)=f_H(x)+\delta_s(x),\qquad x\in\mathcal X,\] with a joint prior over \(f_H\) and the discrepancies \(\{\delta_s\}\); correlations may be encoded directly rather than by independent discrepancies. Given data \(\mathcal D_n\), a resource-aware query rule chooses \[(x_{n+1},s_{n+1})\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{(x,s)}\frac{\mathbb E[J_H(\mathcal D_n\cup\{(x,s,Y_s(x))\})-J_H(\mathcal D_n)\mid\mathcal D_n]}{c_s(x)},\] subject to the remaining budget. The terminal design is selected using the posterior for \(f_H\), not by treating a reduced model as exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model each simulation or reduced model through its dependence on the physical response, then query the design-source pair offering greatest expected physical-design value per cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Fidelity Engineering Design

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record combines a discrepancy representation with a cost-normalized query algorithm and terminal recommendation, so representation does not fully describe its mathematical role. An authoritative multi-fidelity engineering-design source is needed before deciding whether the leaf should contain the representation or the scheduling algorithm.

children.title: Resource-Aware Hyperparameter Optimization
children.top_down_role: Configuration search using partial training, early stopping, transfer, and parallel workers.

assumptions_latex: Configurations lie in \(\mathcal X\), resource levels lie in a finite ordered set \(\mathcal R\), and full resource is \(r_{\max}\).
An observation \(Y(x,r)\) has known or modeled cost \(c(x,r)>0\) and is jointly modeled across configurations and resource levels.
At most \(W\) evaluations may run simultaneously under total budget \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure allocates partial training resources adaptively and returns the configuration with best posterior full-resource performance.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cost-aware multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization with asynchronous worker constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asynchronous multi-fidelity configuration search with partial training and early stopping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a joint surrogate for \(Y(x,r)\) from any initial evaluations. Whenever a worker becomes free, form the admissible set of new starts, promotions, and resumptions whose costs fit the remaining budget. For each \((x,r)\), compute the expected increase \(V_n(x,r)\) in a fixed terminal value for the full-resource objective, integrating pending evaluations under their joint predictive law, and dispatch \[(x,r)\in\operatorname*{argmax}\frac{V_n(x,r)}{c(x,r)}.\] Stop a partial run when no admissible continuation has positive value per cost. Continue until budget \(C\) is exhausted or no action remains, and output \(\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb E[f(x)\mid\mathcal D]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As workers free up, start, promote, resume, or stop configurations according to expected full-training decision value per cost, then recommend the best posterior full-resource configuration.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Aware Hyperparameter Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Resource-Aware Hyperparameter Optimization, but no source supports this particular asynchronous value-per-cost procedure. Promotion, resumption, early stopping, pending-evaluation integration, and the full-resource terminal value are underspecified relative to established algorithms and require authoritative sourcing.

children.title: Adaptive Scientific Experimentation
children.top_down_role: Selection of conditions, instruments, resolutions, replication, and stopping.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a measurable design space and \(\mathcal A\) is a finite or measurable set of experimental configurations.
Each configuration \(a=(x,q,m,r)\in\mathcal A\) specifies conditions, resolution, instrument or fidelity, and replication, with known positive cost \(c(a)\).
Observations follow a specified likelihood and update a posterior distribution over the scientific response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_t\) is selected adaptively and the procedure returns the terminal decision \(\widehat x_\tau\).

notation.meaning: Utility of an experimental configuration under the current posterior

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic Bayesian sequential design with joint condition, instrument, resolution, replication, and stopping choices.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 A simple modeling framework for sequential decision problems p. 47
5. Parametric Optimization: Stochastic Gradients and Adaptive Search p. 71
source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a prior \(\Pi_0\) and an empty history \(\mathcal F_0\). At stage \(t\), compute a posterior utility \(U_t(a)\) for each feasible \(a\in\mathcal A\), incorporating expected scientific value, cost, and remaining resources, and choose \[a_t\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{a\in\mathcal A_t}U_t(a).\] Execute \(a_t\), append its observation and realized cost to \(\mathcal F_t\), and update the posterior. Stop at the first \(t\) satisfying a prespecified posterior-precision, decision-loss, or budget condition; denote this stopping time by \(\tau\). Output a terminal decision \(\widehat x_\tau\) minimizing the posterior expected scientific loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly choose the feasible experiment with greatest posterior utility, update beliefs from its result, and stop when precision, decision-loss, or budget criteria are met.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Scientific Experimentation
