children.title: Guarantee-Complexity-Robustness Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Guarantee and failure families specific to structured and resource-aware Bayesian optimization.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Theoretical Analysis; Effect of Unknown Hyperparameters; Extensions and Related Settings

children.title: Optimization Performance Criteria
children.top_down_role: Guarantees distinguished by terminal, cumulative, cost-indexed, and wall-clock objectives.

children.title: Terminal Recommendation Regret Family
children.top_down_role: Terminal-quality guarantee families.

children.title: Simple Regret
children.top_down_role: Terminal loss indexed by the quality of a selected candidate.

knowledge_statements.title: Simple Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization convention; regret is based on the best latent objective value among evaluated designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization problem, the simple regret after \(n\) evaluations is \[r_n^{\mathrm s}:=f^*-\max_{1\le t\le n}f(x_t),\qquad f^*:=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x).\] Equivalently, if \(x_n^{\mathrm{best}}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le t\le n}f(x_t)\), then \(r_n^{\mathrm s}=f^*-f(x_n^{\mathrm{best}})\). This definition uses latent objective values even when the algorithm observes noisy measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple regret is the optimal value minus the best true objective value among the first n evaluated designs.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is maximized and attains \(f^*=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\).
The algorithm has evaluated \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathcal X\), where \(n\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_n^{\mathrm s}=f^*-\max_{1\le t\le n}f(x_t)\ge0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard maximization-form definition of simple regret

children.title: Recommendation Regret
children.top_down_role: Terminal loss tied to the decision rule producing the final recommendation.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is maximized and attains \(f^*=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\).
After observing data \(\mathcal D_n\), the decision rule recommends \(\widehat x_n\in\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_n^{\mathrm{rec}}=f^*-f(\widehat x_n)\ge 0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: terminal decision regret distinguished from best-sampled simple regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal regret of an arbitrary data-dependent recommendation, which need not have been evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat x_n=\delta_n(\mathcal D_n)\) be the design recommended by a measurable terminal decision rule \(\delta_n\). Its recommendation regret is \[r_n^{\mathrm{rec}}:=f^*-f(\widehat x_n),\qquad f^*:=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x).\] Unlike best-observed simple regret, this criterion permits \(\widehat x_n\notin\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\). For a random objective, noisy data, or randomized rule, \(r_n^{\mathrm{rec}}\) is a random variable; expected, high-probability, and posterior versions must specify the probability law being used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recommendation regret is the optimal value minus the true value of the algorithm's terminal, possibly unevaluated, recommendation.
knowledge_statements.title: Recommendation Regret

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise, distinguishes a terminal recommendation from the best sampled design, and fits the leaf. An inspectable authoritative citation is still required.

children.title: Observed-Incumbent Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Terminal guarantees for recommendations restricted to observed candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Observed-Incumbent Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability guarantees for a terminal incumbent constrained to previously evaluated designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An observed-incumbent guarantee specifies a measurable incumbent rule \(I_n\in\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) and, for each \(\delta\in(0,1)\), establishes a bound \[\mathbb P\!\left(f^*-f(I_n)\le\varepsilon_n(\delta)\right)\ge1-\delta.\] Under exact observations one may choose \(I_n\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le t\le n}f(x_t)\), in which case its regret equals simple regret. Under noisy observations, the incumbent rule and the probability law must be specified explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An observed-incumbent guarantee bounds the true regret of a specified previously evaluated design, with the incumbent rule, noise model, and governing probability law stated explicitly.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) attains its maximum \(f^*\).
The incumbent \(I_n\) is a measurable member of \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\).
A probability law \(\mathbb P\) governing observations and algorithmic randomization is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(f^*-f(I_n)\le\varepsilon_n(\delta))\ge1-\delta\).

children.title: Posterior-Decision Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Terminal guarantees for recommendations derived from posterior decision summaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior-Decision Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior-probability and posterior-risk certificates for a terminal decision under a specified Bayesian model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f^*:=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\). For \(\delta\in(0,1)\), a posterior decision certificate at level \(1-\delta\) is a data-dependent pair \((\widehat x_n,\varepsilon_n)\), with \(\varepsilon_n\ge0\), satisfying \[\Pi_n\!\left(f^*-f(\widehat x_n)\le\varepsilon_n\mid\mathcal D_n\right)\ge1-\delta.\] An expected-loss certificate with threshold \(\rho_n\ge0\) satisfies \[\mathbb E_{\Pi_n}\!\left[f^*-f(\widehat x_n)\mid\mathcal D_n\right]\le\rho_n.\] These are guarantees relative to the stated prior and likelihood and do not imply frequentist coverage without an additional calibration result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A posterior-decision certificate bounds terminal regret in posterior probability or posterior expectation, conditional on the observed data and stated Bayesian model.
assumptions_latex: A prior on \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) and a likelihood for \(\mathcal D_n\) define a posterior distribution \(\Pi_n(\cdot\mid\mathcal D_n)\).
The posterior assigns probability one to functions attaining \(f^*:=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\).
The terminal recommendation \(\widehat x_n\) and thresholds \(\varepsilon_n,\rho_n\ge0\) are measurable with respect to \(\mathcal D_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_n(f^*-f(\widehat x_n)\le\varepsilon_n\mid\mathcal D_n)\ge1-\delta\) or \(\mathbb E_{\Pi_n}[f^*-f(\widehat x_n)\mid\mathcal D_n]\le\rho_n\).

children.title: Cumulative Regret
children.top_down_role: Guarantee families valuing performance throughout search.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is maximized and attains \(f^*\).
The sequential policy evaluates \(x_t\in\mathcal X\) at rounds \(t=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted finite-horizon regret, valuing objective performance at every evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The instantaneous regret of evaluation \(x_t\) is \(r_t:=f^*-f(x_t)\), where \(f^*:=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\). The cumulative regret through round \(n\) is \[R_n:=\sum_{t=1}^{n}r_t=\sum_{t=1}^{n}\bigl(f^*-f(x_t)\bigr).\] If observations or actions are random, \(R_n\) is random and guarantees may concern \(\mathbb E[R_n]\) or \(\mathbb P(R_n\le b_n)\). Sublinear cumulative regret, \(R_n/n\to0\), is equivalent to vanishing average instantaneous regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative regret sums the objective gap incurred at every evaluation; sublinear cumulative regret means the average gap vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Cumulative Regret

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximization-form definition and content kind fit the cumulative-regret leaf, and the sublinearity statement is correct. An inspectable authoritative source is missing.

children.title: Structured-Dimension Regret
children.top_down_role: Guarantees depending on additive, sparse, latent, or discrete complexity.

assumptions_latex: A structured surrogate model has effective complexity parameter \(d_{\mathrm{eff}}\) and maximum information gain \(\gamma_n(d_{\mathrm{eff}})\).
On a confidence event of probability at least \(1-\delta\), the policy's instantaneous regret satisfies \(r_t\le 2\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\sigma_{t-1}(x_t)\).
The posterior variances satisfy \(\sum_{t=1}^n\sigma_{t-1}^2(x_t)\le C_0\gamma_n(d_{\mathrm{eff}})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_n\le2\sqrt{C_0n\beta_n\gamma_n(d_{\mathrm{eff}})}\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: Maximum information gain through n observations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic information-gain bound exposing additive, sparse, latent, or discrete effective complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\beta_t\) is nondecreasing. On the stated confidence event, Cauchy--Schwarz gives \[R_n=\sum_{t=1}^n r_t\le 2\sqrt{\beta_n}\sum_{t=1}^n\sigma_{t-1}(x_t)\le2\sqrt{C_0n\beta_n\gamma_n(d_{\mathrm{eff}})}.\] Hence the regret depends on ambient dimension only through the structured information complexity \(\gamma_n(d_{\mathrm{eff}})\). The meaning of \(d_{\mathrm{eff}}\) must be instantiated by the model, such as additive component size, sparsity, latent dimension, or the cardinality and kernel complexity of a discrete structure class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When confidence widths and posterior variances obey standard information-gain bounds, cumulative regret scales with structured effective complexity rather than raw ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Structured-Dimension Regret

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the confidence or information-gain inequalities. The statement also contains proof text and overstates that ambient dimension enters only through \(\gamma_n\), since \(\beta_n\) and \(C_0\) may depend on the model or dimension.

children.title: Expenditure-Indexed Regret Family
children.top_down_role: Performance indexed by expenditure rather than observation count.

children.title: Cost-Normalized Regret
children.top_down_role: Regret assessed relative to resource expenditure.

assumptions_latex: Each action \(x_t\) has realized positive cost \(c_t>0\).
The maximization objective attains value \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline R_n^{\mathrm{cost}}=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^n c_t(f^*-f(x_t))}{\sum_{t=1}^n c_t}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-weighted average objective gap; alternative uses of “cost-normalized regret” require explicit conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_n:=\sum_{t=1}^n c_t\) be total expenditure. Define cost-weighted cumulative regret and its normalized form by \[R_n^{\mathrm{cost}}:=\sum_{t=1}^n c_t\bigl(f^*-f(x_t)\bigr),\qquad \overline R_n^{\mathrm{cost}}:=\frac{R_n^{\mathrm{cost}}}{C_n}.\] Thus \(\overline R_n^{\mathrm{cost}}\) is the objective gap averaged with respect to units of expenditure. This convention differs from dividing unweighted cumulative regret by total cost; the weighting and denominator must therefore be stated whenever the term is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cost-normalized regret is the expenditure-weighted average objective gap, with the weighting convention stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Normalized Regret

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit cost-weighted convention is internally coherent and the definition kind fits the leaf, but “cost-normalized regret” is not canonical. A source supporting this selected convention is necessary.

children.title: Budget-Indexed Regret
children.top_down_role: Regret assessed at specified resource-budget levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Budget-Indexed Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal best-sampled regret indexed by expenditure rather than evaluation count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_0:=0\) and \(C_n:=\sum_{t=1}^n c_t\). Define the budget stopping index by \[N(B):=\max\{n\ge0:C_n\le B\}.\] When \(N(B)\ge1\), the budget-indexed simple regret is \[r(B):=f^*-\max_{1\le t\le N(B)}f(x_t).\] A recommendation version replaces the sampled maximum by \(f(\widehat x_{N(B)})\). This convention excludes an evaluation whose completion would make cumulative cost exceed \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Budget-indexed regret measures terminal optimization error after completing the evaluations whose cumulative cost does not exceed the available budget.
assumptions_latex: An infinite sequential action stream is defined, action \(t\) incurs cost \(c_t>0\), \(C_0:=0\), and \(C_n:=\sum_{t=1}^n c_t\).
A budget \(B>0\) is fixed, \(N(B)\) is finite, and at least one action is affordable.
The maximization objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) attains \(f^*:=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r(B)=f^*-\max_{1\le t\le N(B)}f(x_t)\), where \(N(B)=\max\{n\ge0:C_n\le B\}\).

notation.meaning: Number of completed evaluations within budget B

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stopping-index definition induced by cumulative positive costs

children.title: Expenditure-Horizon Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Performance comparisons across monetary, computational, or temporal horizons.

knowledge_statements.title: Expenditure-Horizon Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic conversion between evaluation horizons and expenditure horizons under uniformly bounded costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\ge0\), bounded costs imply \[n c_{\min}\le C_n\le n c_{\max}.\] Consequently, for every \(B\ge c_{\max}\), \[\left\lfloor\frac{B}{c_{\max}}\right\rfloor\le N(B)\le\left\lfloor\frac{B}{c_{\min}}\right\rfloor.\] If the simple regret along the same evaluation sequence satisfies \(r_n^{\mathrm s}\le g(n)\) for a nonincreasing deterministic function \(g\), then \[r(B)\le g\!\left(\left\lfloor B/c_{\max}\right\rfloor\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform lower and upper evaluation-cost bounds convert an expenditure budget into evaluation-count bounds and transfer a monotone horizon regret guarantee to the budget horizon.
assumptions_latex: An infinite action sequence has costs satisfying \(0<c_{\min}\le c_t\le c_{\max}<\infty\).
Cumulative expenditure is \(C_0:=0\), \(C_n:=\sum_{t=1}^n c_t\), and \(N(B):=\max\{n\ge0:C_n\le B\}\).
For the regret transfer, \(B\ge c_{\max}\) and the same evaluation sequence satisfies \(r_n^{\mathrm s}\le g(n)\) for a nonincreasing deterministic function \(g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lfloor B/c_{\max}\rfloor\le N(B)\le\lfloor B/c_{\min}\rfloor\), and \(r(B)\le g(\lfloor B/c_{\max}\rfloor)\) under the stated horizon guarantee.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: deterministic comparison from uniformly bounded positive costs

children.title: Cost-Misspecification Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Guarantee sensitivity to inaccurate resource-cost representations.

assumptions_latex: True costs \(c_t>0\) and modeled costs \(\widehat c_t>0\) satisfy \(\alpha c_t\le\widehat c_t\le\beta c_t\) for fixed \(0<\alpha\le\beta<\infty\).
Budget feasibility is enforced using modeled cumulative cost \(\widehat C_n:=\sum_{t=1}^n\widehat c_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha C_n\le\widehat C_n\le\beta C_n\); without finite multiplicative bounds, modeled-budget guarantees need not control true expenditure.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: deterministic sensitivity boundary from multiplicative cost distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robustness boundary for transferring modeled-cost budget guarantees to true expenditure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Summing the pointwise distortion inequalities yields \[\alpha C_n\le\widehat C_n\le\beta C_n.\] Hence \(\widehat C_n\le B\) guarantees only \(C_n\le B/\alpha\), while \(C_n\le B/\beta\) guarantees \(\widehat C_n\le B\). This multiplicative transfer fails without a uniform lower distortion bound: for example, if \(c_t=1\) and \(\widehat c_t=2^{-t}\), then \(\widehat C_n<1\) for every finite \(n\), whereas \(C_n=n\) is unbounded. Thus a fixed modeled budget can permit arbitrarily large true expenditure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicatively accurate cost models yield rescaled budget guarantees; systematic underestimation without a uniform bound can hide unbounded true expenditure.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Misspecification Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the sensitivity leaf, and the multiplicative transfer and counterexample are mathematically correct. However, the record contains derivational proof text and supplies no inspectable source for the stated robustness boundary.

children.title: Structured Search Discovery Principles
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic discovery and recommendation guarantees across structured regimes.

children.title: Observation-Regime Consistency Classes
children.top_down_role: Consistency families under deterministic and stochastic evaluations.

children.title: Exact-Observation Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency guarantees for deterministic evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Observation Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-sampled consistency under exact observations, continuity, compactness, and asymptotically dense evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the fill distance by \[h_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\min_{1\le t\le n}d(x,x_t).\] If \(h_n\to0\), then the best-sampled simple regret satisfies \[r_n^{\mathrm s}:=f^*-\max_{1\le t\le n}f(x_t)\longrightarrow0.\] Because observations are exact, an incumbent selected by the largest observed value is a true best-sampled point and has the same regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous objective on a compact metric space, exact observations on increasingly dense designs make best-sampled simple regret converge to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a compact metric space and \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, so \(f^*:=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\) exists.
Observations are exact: \(y_t=f(x_t)\).
The fill distance \(h_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\min_{1\le t\le n}d(x,x_t)\) satisfies \(h_n\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_n^{\mathrm s}=f^*-\max_{1\le t\le n}f(x_t)\to0\).

notation.meaning: Fill distance of the evaluated set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: compactness, continuity, and dense exact sampling imply best-value consistency

children.title: Noisy-Observation Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency guarantees under stochastic evaluation noise.

knowledge_statements.title: Noisy-Observation Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency of recommendations under additive, conditionally unbiased observation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a compact decision space, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) attain its minimum \(f^*\), and let an adaptive algorithm observe \(Y_t=f(x_t)+\varepsilon_t\), where \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0\) and \(\sup_t\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_t^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]<\infty\). If \(\widehat x_n\) is its recommendation after \(n\) observations, the algorithm is noisy-observation consistent for \(f\) when \[f(\widehat x_n)-f^*\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathbb P}0.\] Strong consistency replaces convergence in probability by almost-sure convergence. Consistency over a function class requires this conclusion for every member of that class under the stated noise model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recommendations are consistent when their objective-value gap converges to zero despite conditionally unbiased, bounded-variance observation noise.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact and \(f\) attains its minimum.
\(Y_t=f(x_t)+\varepsilon_t\) with conditionally zero-mean, uniformly bounded-variance noise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\widehat x_n)-f^*\to0\) in probability, or almost surely for strong consistency.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22

children.title: Observation-Regime Robustness
children.top_down_role: Guarantee sensitivity when the assumed observation regime differs from operating conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Observation-Regime Robustness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform consistency across a specified family of admissible observation laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_n(P,f)=f(\widehat x_n)-\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) be the simple regret when observations follow \(P\). For a function class \(\mathcal G\) and observation-law family \(\mathcal P\), an algorithm is observation-regime robust if, for every \(\eta>0\), \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{f\in\mathcal G}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(f)}P\!\left(r_n(P,f)>\eta\right)=0.\] Pointwise consistency under each fixed \(P\) does not imply this property: robustness requires a common sample size controlling the error probability uniformly over all admitted noise distributions, missingness mechanisms, or fidelity regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robustness strengthens pointwise consistency to uniform convergence over an explicitly specified family of observation regimes and objectives.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P(f)\) contains only observation laws under which the algorithm and regret are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal G}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(f)}P(r_n(P,f)>\eta)\to0\) for every \(\eta>0\).

notation.meaning: Admissible observation laws for objective f.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform convergence property is coherent and fits the leaf, but no citation supports this particular robustness definition or the admissible observation-law formulation.

children.title: Localized-Search Convergence
children.top_down_role: Guarantees and limitations for trust-region and partition methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Localized-Search Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient convergence result for nested trust regions or partition cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be compact, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let \(R_n\subseteq X\) be the active region of a localized search. Suppose that, almost surely, some global minimizer \(x^*\) belongs to every \(R_n\) after a finite random index, \(\operatorname{diam}(R_n)\to0\), and the returned point \(\widehat x_n\in R_n\) satisfies \[f(\widehat x_n)\leq \inf_{x\in R_n}f(x)+\epsilon_n,\qquad \epsilon_n\to0.\] Then \(d(\widehat x_n,x^*)\to0\) and \(f(\widehat x_n)\to f(x^*)\) almost surely. Thus localization alone is insufficient unless the retained regions eventually contain a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking localized regions yield global convergence when they eventually retain a global minimizer and are solved with vanishing local error.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is compact and \(f\) is continuous.
Eventually \(x^*\in R_n\), while \(\operatorname{diam}(R_n)\to0\).
The local optimization error \(\epsilon_n\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(\widehat x_n,x^*)\to0\) and \(f(\widehat x_n)\to f(x^*)\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: Active trust region or partition cell.

children.title: Discrete-Domain Identification Classes
children.top_down_role: Eventual identification guarantees on discrete structured domains.

children.title: Finite-Domain Identification
children.top_down_role: Eventual identification guarantees over finite candidate sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Domain Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-confidence identification of an optimizer in an explicitly finite decision domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_K\}\), let observations from decision \(x\) have mean \(f(x)\), and assume the minimizer \(x^*\) is unique. A sequential procedure with stopping time \(\tau\) and output \(\widehat x\) is \(\delta\)-correct for finite-domain identification if \[\mathbb P_f(\tau<\infty)=1,\qquad \mathbb P_f(\widehat x=x^*)\geq1-\delta.\] A family of such procedures is consistent when its error probability tends to zero as its sampling budget tends to infinity. Its identification complexity is the number of samples, or expected number \(\mathbb E_f[\tau]\), required to meet the confidence requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-domain identification returns the unique best member of a finite set with a prescribed probability of correctness.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite and every decision has a well-defined observation distribution.
The mean objective has a unique minimizer \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P_f(\widehat x=x^*)\geq1-\delta\) with almost-sure finite stopping.

source_refs.locator: 7.3 Direct Policy Search for Finite Alternatives p. 256

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Direct Policy Search for Finite Alternatives p. 256

children.title: Combinatorial-Domain Identification
children.top_down_role: Identification guarantees for structured discrete configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial-Domain Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification over an implicitly represented family of discrete feasible structures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\{0,1\}^m\) encode feasible combinatorial objects, and let \(F(x)\) be their unknown mean loss. A procedure with stopping time \(\tau\) and output \(\widehat x\in\mathcal X\) performs \(\delta\)-correct combinatorial-domain identification when \[\mathbb P_F\!\left(\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}F(x)\right)\geq1-\delta,\qquad \mathbb P_F(\tau<\infty)=1.\] The definition permits \(\mathcal X\) to be exponentially large, provided feasibility and optimization are accessed through a compact structural description or an exact combinatorial oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combinatorial identification finds an optimal feasible discrete structure with high probability without requiring explicit enumeration of all structures.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\subseteq\{0,1\}^m\) is nonempty.
Every feasible structure has a well-defined mean loss \(F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat x\) is optimal over \(\mathcal X\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: Unknown mean loss on feasible structures.

source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

source_witnesses.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

children.title: Discrete-Structure Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dependence of identification difficulty on discrete domain structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Structure Scaling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes enumerative and structure-exploiting complexity for growing discrete domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence \(\mathcal X_m\subseteq\{0,1\}^m\), an identification method is in the enumerative regime when its worst-case storage, oracle calls, or samples scale as \(\Omega(|\mathcal X_m|)\). It is structure-scaling when these resources are bounded by \(\operatorname{poly}(m,\log(1/\delta),1/\Delta_m)\), where \(\Delta_m\) is the smallest relevant positive optimality gap. If \(|\mathcal X_m|=\exp(\Theta(m))\), polynomial dependence on \(|\mathcal X_m|\) is exponential in the structural dimension, whereas polynomial dependence on \(m\) is not. Such a bound must include the cost of any feasibility or combinatorial optimization oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling is enumerative when it depends on the number of structures, and structure-exploiting when polynomial in their compact description and accuracy parameters.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X_m\) has a structural description of dimension \(m\).
\(\Delta_m>0\) denotes the identification-relevant optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(|\mathcal X_m|=\exp(\Theta(m))\), polynomial scaling in \(m\) and polynomial scaling in \(|\mathcal X_m|\) are qualitatively different regimes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The enumerative-versus-structural distinction is plausible, but the proposed polynomial resource criterion and treatment of oracle costs constitute a substantive scaling taxonomy with no cited support.

children.title: Constrained-Multiobjective Identification Pair
children.top_down_role: Identification guarantees for constrained and multiobjective searches.

children.title: Feasible-Set Identification
children.top_down_role: Recovery guarantees for admissible regions under constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform high-probability classification of constraint feasibility away from a boundary band.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a decision space, let \(g_j:X\to\mathbb R\) for \(j=1,\ldots,q\), and define \(F=\{x\in X:g_j(x)\leq0\ \text{for all }j\}\). An estimator \(\widehat F_n\) achieves \((\epsilon,\delta)\)-feasible-set identification if, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), \[\{x:\max_j g_j(x)\leq-\epsilon\}\subseteq\widehat F_n\subseteq\{x:\max_j g_j(x)\leq\epsilon\}.\] Thus every point separated from the constraint boundary by more than \(\epsilon\) is classified correctly; points inside the boundary band may remain unresolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible-set identification correctly classifies all decisions lying outside an epsilon-wide uncertainty band around the constraint boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(F=\{x:g_j(x)\leq0\text{ for every }j\}\) is the true feasible set.
\(\epsilon\geq0\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:\max_jg_j(x)\leq-\epsilon\}\subseteq\widehat F_n\subseteq\{x:\max_jg_j(x)\leq\epsilon\}\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

source_refs.locator: 1.7.1 The Feasible Set and Solvability p. 54

source_witnesses.locator: 1.7.1 The Feasible Set and Solvability p. 54

children.title: Pareto-Set Identification
children.top_down_role: Recovery guarantees for nondominated solutions in multiobjective searches.

knowledge_statements.title: Pareto-Set Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistent recovery of constrained nondominated decisions in decision-space distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be compact, let \(F\subseteq X\) be the feasible set, and let \(h:F\to\mathbb R^p\) be minimized componentwise. Define the Pareto set \(P^*\) as the feasible points for which no \(z\in F\) satisfies \(h_i(z)\leq h_i(x)\) for every \(i\) and \(h_j(z)<h_j(x)\) for some \(j\). An estimator \(\widehat P_n\subseteq F\) consistently identifies the Pareto set when \[d_H(\widehat P_n,P^*)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathbb P}0,\] where \(d_H\) is Hausdorff distance. Almost-sure convergence defines strong identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pareto-set identification requires the estimated feasible nondominated decisions to converge to the true Pareto set in Hausdorff distance.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is compact and \(P^*\) is nonempty and compact.
All objectives \(h_i\) are minimized componentwise on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_H(\widehat P_n,P^*)\to0\) in probability.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The decision-space Hausdorff formulation is coherent, but it is one particular notion of Pareto-set identification and has no source establishing that this is the intended consistency criterion.

children.title: Constraint–Objective Interaction
children.top_down_role: Identification effects arising from coupled feasibility and objective uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint–Objective Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposes constrained identification error into feasibility and objective-ordering errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P^*=\operatorname{Pareto}(F,h)\), and let an estimator form \(\widehat P=\operatorname{Pareto}(\widehat F,\widehat h)\). For any tolerance criterion, suppose correct feasible-set classification is event \(E_F\), and correct objective dominance comparisons on the relevant feasible candidates is event \(E_h\). Then \[E_F\cap E_h\subseteq\{\widehat P\text{ satisfies the target Pareto-identification criterion}\},\] and consequently \[\mathbb P(\widehat P\text{ fails})\leq\mathbb P(E_F^c)+\mathbb P(E_h^c).\] Hence objective accuracy on confidently infeasible points is irrelevant, while constraint errors near competitive points can directly create or remove estimated Pareto solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constrained Pareto error is controlled jointly by feasibility classification and objective-ordering error, with failure probability bounded by their sum.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat P\) is obtained by Pareto filtering estimated feasible candidates.
Events \(E_F\) and \(E_h\) jointly imply the chosen identification criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\widehat P\text{ fails})\leq\mathbb P(E_F^c)+\mathbb P(E_h^c)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The union-bound conclusion follows from the stipulated event implication, but the substantive choice of feasibility and dominance events and the resulting interaction claim lack an authoritative source.

children.title: Resource-Aware Evaluation Guarantee System
children.top_down_role: Guarantee families quantifying information loss, delays, source bias, and cost savings.

children.title: Batch Information-Loss Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Statistical cost of selecting points without intermediate feedback.

knowledge_statements.title: Batch Information-Loss Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact information accounting for points selected without within-batch feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be the latent quantity of interest and let \(Y_A=(Y_x)_{x\in A}\) be observations in a batch \(A\), conditionally independent given \(Z\). The batch information satisfies the chain rule \[I(Z;Y_A)=\sum_{k=1}^{|A|}I\!\left(Z;Y_{x_k}\mid Y_{x_1},\ldots,Y_{x_{k-1}}\right).\] Relative to summing stale marginal scores, the redundancy loss is \[L(A)=\sum_{x\in A}I(Z;Y_x)-I(Z;Y_A)\geq0\] whenever the information set function is submodular. Therefore selecting multiple points without intermediate feedback cannot realize more information than the sum of their individually assessed marginal gains; diversity controls the loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Batch information equals sequential conditional gains, while stale individual scores overcount information by a nonnegative redundancy term under submodularity.
assumptions_latex: Observations \((Y_x)_{x\in A}\) are conditionally independent given \(Z\).
The set function \(A\mapsto I(Z;Y_A)\) is submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(Z;Y_A)=\sum_k I(Z;Y_{x_k}\mid Y_{x_1},\ldots,Y_{x_{k-1}})\) and \(L(A)\geq0\).

notation.meaning: Latent function or parameter of interest.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chain rule and redundancy expression are mathematically coherent, but the model conditions ensuring submodularity and the interpretation as a batch information-loss guarantee require a specific source.

children.title: Delayed-Feedback Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Performance under bounded or stochastic delays.

knowledge_statements.title: Delayed-Feedback Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior-uncertainty inflation under observations pending because of delayed feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider Gaussian-process observations with independent Gaussian noise. At decision time \(t\), let \(O_t\) be observed indices and \(P_t\) pending indices. Write \(\sigma_{O_t}(x)\) for the stale posterior standard deviation and \(\sigma_{O_t\cup P_t}(x)\) for the standard deviation after pending outcomes are revealed. If \[I(f;Y_{P_t}\mid Y_{O_t})\leq C\] for every \(t\), then for every candidate \(x\), \[\sigma_{O_t}(x)\leq e^C\sigma_{O_t\cup P_t}(x).\] Thus bounded conditional information in delayed observations yields a uniform multiplicative inflation factor for stale uncertainty bounds; unbounded pending information precludes this guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If pending observations contain at most C conditional information, stale Gaussian-process uncertainty is inflated by at most an exponential factor.
assumptions_latex: The surrogate is a Gaussian process with independent Gaussian observation noise.
\(I(f;Y_{P_t}\mid Y_{O_t})\leq C\) uniformly in \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{O_t}(x)\leq e^C\sigma_{O_t\cup P_t}(x)\) for every \(t\) and \(x\).

notation.meaning: Indices observed by decision time t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponential standard-deviation inflation factor is model- and convention-sensitive and needs an exact Gaussian-process delayed-feedback lemma. Because the statement is an if-then guarantee, theorem may be more appropriate than property once sourced.

children.title: Parallel Speedup Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs among worker utilization, sample efficiency, and elapsed time.

children.title: Wall-Clock Speedup
children.top_down_role: Elapsed-time gains attributable to concurrent evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Wall-Clock Speedup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Idealized elapsed-time bound for synchronous parallel evaluations with serial acquisition overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(N\) evaluations are required, each takes time \(c_e\), acquisition and synchronization contribute serial time \(T_s\), and \(p\) identical workers execute evaluations synchronously without failures. Then the wall-clock time obeys \[T_p\geq T_s+c_e\left\lceil\frac{N}{p}\right\rceil,\] so the speedup over \(T_1=T_s+Nc_e\) satisfies \[S_p=\frac{T_1}{T_p}\leq\frac{T_s+Nc_e}{T_s+c_e\lceil N/p\rceil}\leq\min\!\left\{p,1+\frac{Nc_e}{T_s}\right\}.\] Any increase in required evaluations caused by batching must replace \(N\) by the parallel method's own sample requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel wall-clock speedup is limited by worker count, serial overhead, synchronization, and any extra evaluations required by batching.
assumptions_latex: There are \(p\) identical reliable workers and each evaluation takes time \(c_e\).
Acquisition and synchronization require serial time \(T_s\).
The parallel procedure requires \(N\) evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_p\leq (T_s+Nc_e)/(T_s+c_e\lceil N/p\rceil)\leq\min\{p,1+Nc_e/T_s\}\).

notation.meaning: Wall-clock speedup relative to one worker.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The idealized scheduling bound fits the wall-clock complexity container, but it has no citation and the final bound containing division by T_s requires the explicit assumption T_s>0.

children.title: Parallelism Limits
children.top_down_role: Structural limits on useful evaluation concurrency.

assumptions_latex: A fraction \(\rho\in(0,1]\) of serial wall-clock work is unaffected by the worker count.
The remaining fraction \(1-\rho\) is perfectly divisible among \(q\ge 1\) identical workers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The speedup satisfies \(S_q\le (\rho+(1-\rho)/q)^{-1}\) and \(\lim_{q\to\infty}S_q\le 1/\rho\).

notation.meaning: Serial fraction of baseline wall-clock time

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Amdahl-type decomposition gives a standard upper bound on parallel speedup.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amdahl-type limit for ideal worker parallelization with nonzero serial policy overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the one-worker wall-clock time be normalized to \(1\), with serial fraction \(\rho\in(0,1]\) and perfectly parallelizable fraction \(1-\rho\). With \(q\ge1\) identical workers, the runtime is bounded below by \(T_q=\rho+(1-\rho)/q\). Hence the attainable speedup obeys \[S_q=\frac{T_1}{T_q}\le \frac{1}{\rho+(1-\rho)/q},\qquad \limsup_{q\to\infty}S_q\le\frac{1}{\rho}.\] Thus any positive serial fraction imposes a finite parallelism limit, even when evaluations themselves parallelize without communication or load imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero serial fraction caps worker speedup: even infinitely many workers cannot improve runtime by more than the reciprocal serial fraction.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallelism Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits Parallelism Limits, and the Amdahl-type ceiling is standard. However, no citation is supplied. The statement also calls T_q both a lower bound and the modeled runtime; an authoritative source or corrected formulation must clarify whether equality holds under the ideal decomposition or whether additional overhead makes the displayed expression only a lower bound.

children.title: Worker-Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Guarantee behavior as available worker capacity changes.

assumptions_latex: Each cycle dispatches \(q\) evaluations of common duration \(\tau>0\).
Selecting and dispatching the batch costs \(a(q)\ge0\) units of serial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Throughput is \(R(q)=q/(\tau+a(q))\), with ideal, proportional-loss, and saturation regimes determined by \(a(q)/\tau\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Throughput follows from a cycle-time accounting identity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worker regimes classified by policy overhead relative to evaluation duration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose one synchronous cycle spends \(a(q)\) time selecting and dispatching \(q\) evaluations, followed by evaluation time \(\tau\). Its steady-state throughput is \[R(q)=\frac{q}{a(q)+\tau}.\] If \(a(q)/\tau\to0\), then \(R(q)\sim q/\tau\), giving asymptotically ideal worker scaling. If \(a(q)/\tau\to c\in(0,\infty)\), throughput remains linear but loses the factor \(1/(1+c)\). If \(a(q)/q\to c>0\), then \(R(q)\to1/c\), so throughput saturates. Superlinear policy cost makes additional workers eventually reduce throughput.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worker scaling is ideal when policy overhead is negligible, proportionally degraded when comparable to evaluation time, and saturated when overhead grows linearly with workers.
knowledge_statements.title: Worker-Scaling Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role is suitable for Worker-Scaling Regimes, and the throughput identity and three displayed asymptotic regimes are internally consistent. No citation supports the Bayesian-optimization interpretation. Moreover, superlinear growth a(q)/q to infinity implies R(q) tends to zero but does not by itself imply that throughput eventually decreases without an additional eventual-monotonicity assumption.

children.title: Sample-Efficiency Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Losses in evaluation efficiency associated with faster parallel progress.

assumptions_latex: Observations are noiseless.
A batch policy may select repeated locations without conditioning on pending outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A batch of \(q\) repeated evaluations can have the information value of one evaluation, producing a factor-\(q\) sample-efficiency loss.

notation.meaning: Unknown objective value at the repeated location

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Repeated noiseless observations are informationally redundant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete redundancy mechanism showing that wall-clock parallelism need not preserve sample efficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a batch of size \(q\ge2\) evaluate the same location \(x_0\), and let every noiseless observation satisfy \(Y_i=f(x_0)\). Then \(\sigma(Y_{1:q})=\sigma(Y_1)\), so for any latent objective \(f\), \[I(f;Y_{1:q})=I(f;Y_1).\] Consequently, the batch spends \(q\) evaluations while acquiring only one evaluation's information. A sequential policy that conditions after every outcome can instead use the remaining \(q-1\) evaluations elsewhere. Thus unrestricted batch selection admits a worst-case factor-\(q\) loss in information gained per evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel batches can waste samples: repeating one noiseless location q times yields no more information than one evaluation, despite consuming q evaluations.
knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Efficiency Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A failure_boundary is appropriate for Sample-Efficiency Tradeoffs, and repeated noiseless observations generate the same sigma-field. No source is cited. The mutual-information formulation needs conditions ensuring that the quantities and claimed factor comparison are meaningful, and the assertion that a sequential policy can use the remaining evaluations more informatively does not follow without assumptions on the domain and latent objective.

children.title: Fidelity–Bias–Cost Complexity
children.top_down_role: Search complexity organized by auxiliary-source discrepancy and cost.

assumptions_latex: The candidate set \(X\) is finite with \(|X|=M\).
At fidelity \(s\), observations are independent \(\sigma_s\)-sub-Gaussian with mean \(f_s(x)\).
The deterministic bias satisfies \(|f_s(x)-f(x)|\le\zeta_s\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any fidelity with \(\zeta_s\le\varepsilon/4\) attains \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy at cost at most \(c_s\lceil32\sigma_s^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2M/\delta)\rceil\) per uniformly sampled candidate.

notation.meaning: Bias bound and per-query cost of fidelity s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:The bound follows from finite-set sub-Gaussian concentration plus a uniform fidelity-bias bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain cost bound exposing the admissible-fidelity bias threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fidelity \(s\) satisfying \(\zeta_s\le\varepsilon/4\), take \[n_s=\left\lceil\frac{32\sigma_s^2}{\varepsilon^2}\log\frac{2M}{\delta}\right\rceil\] samples at every \(x\in X\), form their means \(\widehat f_s(x)\), and output \(\widehat x\in\arg\max_x\widehat f_s(x)\). With probability at least \(1-\delta\), every sampling error is at most \(\varepsilon/4\), and therefore \(f(x^*)-f(\widehat x)\le\varepsilon\). The evaluation cost is at most \(M c_s n_s\); minimizing this expression over fidelities satisfying the bias threshold gives the best bound within this uniform-sampling scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fidelity is usable only when its bias fits the accuracy target; among usable fidelities, noise and query cost determine total search cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Fidelity–Bias–Cost Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits Fidelity-Bias-Cost Complexity. The finite-set concentration calculation, bias threshold, total cost, and simple-regret conclusion are mutually consistent under the stated sub-Gaussian convention. Nevertheless, the record has no inspectable citation, and the supplied local inventory does not specifically support this multifidelity bound.

children.title: Source-Screening Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Guarantees for retaining useful sources and rejecting harmful ones.

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many auxiliary sources \(s\in\{1,\ldots,S\}\).
Paired discrepancies \(D_{s,i}\) are independent \(\sigma_s\)-sub-Gaussian with mean \(d_s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Simultaneous confidence screening retains every source with \(d_s\le\theta-2r_s\) and rejects every source with \(d_s>\theta\), with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: Mean discrepancy of source s from the target

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Simultaneous sub-Gaussian confidence intervals yield the stated screening separation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability threshold screening from paired target-source discrepancy samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For source \(s\), let \(\widehat d_s=n_s^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}D_{s,i}\) and \[r_s=\sigma_s\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2S/\delta)}{n_s}}.\] Retain \(s\) when \(\widehat d_s+r_s\le\theta\), reject it when \(\widehat d_s-r_s>\theta\), and otherwise leave it undecided. With probability at least \(1-\delta\), all intervals \([\widehat d_s-r_s,\widehat d_s+r_s]\) contain \(d_s\) simultaneously. On this event, every source satisfying \(d_s\le\theta-2r_s\) is retained and every source satisfying \(d_s>\theta\) is rejected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Confidence bounds retain clearly useful low-discrepancy sources, reject sources beyond the discrepancy threshold, and leave insufficiently separated sources undecided.
knowledge_statements.title: Source-Screening Guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits Source-Screening Guarantees, but the rejection conclusion is false for the stated confidence rule. On the simultaneous event, hat d_s-r_s can only be bounded below by d_s-2r_s, so guaranteed rejection requires d_s greater than theta+2r_s, not merely d_s greater than theta. No source is supplied to resolve or support the theorem.

children.title: Computational Complexity Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Internal costs determining whether structural and resource-aware policies remain practical.

children.title: Surrogate Scaling Under Rapid Data Acquisition
children.top_down_role: Inference costs created by parallel or replicated observations.

assumptions_latex: The surrogate is an exact Gaussian process evaluated by dense Cholesky factorization.
A batch contributes \(q\) new observations to an existing data set of size \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact storage is \(\Theta((n+q)^2)\), refactorization costs \(\Theta((n+q)^3)\), and sequential rank-one updates cost \(O(qn^2+q^2n+q^3)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Dense Cholesky storage and arithmetic counts are standard.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense exact-GP scaling when observations arrive rapidly in batches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After assimilating \(q\) observations, an exact dense Gaussian-process surrogate has a covariance matrix of order \(n+q\). Storing it requires \(\Theta((n+q)^2)\) memory, and rebuilding its Cholesky factor requires \(\Theta((n+q)^3)\) arithmetic operations. If observations are incorporated through rank-one Cholesky extensions, the aggregate update cost satisfies \[C_{n,q}=O\!\left(\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}(n+j)^2\right)=O(qn^2+q^2n+q^3).\] Hence sufficiently rapid parallel acquisition can make surrogate maintenance, rather than physical evaluation, the wall-clock bottleneck.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For exact dense Gaussian processes, rapid acquisition creates quadratic memory and cubic refactorization costs; even incremental batch updates grow roughly as q times n squared.
knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate Scaling Under Rapid Data Acquisition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind exactly fits Surrogate Scaling Under Rapid Data Acquisition. The dense-storage, full-factorization, and summed rank-one-extension orders are consistent. No exact-Gaussian-process computational source with a specific locator is cited, so the record cannot pass source review.

children.title: Nested Acquisition-Optimization Cost
children.top_down_role: Inner burden from joint point, source, task, and batch decisions.

assumptions_latex: The acquisition is optimized by exhaustive enumeration over finite point, source, and task sets.
A batch contains \(q\) distinct points and assigns one source-task pair to each point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustive joint acquisition optimization requires \(\binom{M}{q}(ST)^q\) acquisition evaluations.

notation.meaning: Numbers of candidate points, sources, and tasks

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:The count follows directly from enumerating batches and per-point source-task assignments.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case enumeration cost for joint point, source, task, and batch choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(|X|=M\), let there be \(S\) sources and \(T\) tasks, and require a batch of \(q\le M\) distinct points. There are \(\binom{M}{q}\) unordered point batches and \((ST)^q\) source-task assignments for each ordered representation of a fixed batch. Consequently, exhaustive optimization evaluates the joint acquisition at most \[N_{\mathrm{cand}}=\binom{M}{q}(ST)^q\] candidates and costs \(\Theta(C_\alpha N_{\mathrm{cand}})\). The exponential dependence on \(q\) persists even when evaluating one acquisition candidate is constant-time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jointly enumerating points, sources, tasks, and batches is combinatorial, with candidate count equal to a binomial batch factor times one assignment factor per point.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Acquisition-Optimization Cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits Nested Acquisition-Optimization Cost. For a batch viewed as a set of q identifiable points, the count binom(M,q)(ST)^q is valid. The Theta(C_alpha N_cand) assertion additionally requires C_alpha to denote a uniform per-candidate cost bound of matching order. No structured-acquisition source is cited.

children.title: Representation-Learning Overhead
children.top_down_role: Cost of learning embeddings, decompositions, or task relations during search.

assumptions_latex: At each retraining event, a dense \(n\times n\) representation matrix is approximated to rank \(r\).
The factorization algorithm costs \(\Theta(n^2r)\) arithmetic operations and stores \(\Theta(nr)\) numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Retraining after every batch of size \(q\) through \(N\) observations costs \(\Theta(rN^3/q)\) cumulatively.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:The cumulative bound is the sum of stipulated dense low-rank factorization costs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cumulative overhead of repeatedly relearning a dense low-rank representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the representation is relearned whenever the data size reaches \(n_j=jq\), for \(j=1,\ldots,m\), where \(m=N/q\) is integral. If rank-\(r\) learning at size \(n\) costs \(\Theta(n^2r)\), then cumulative representation work is \[C_{\mathrm{rep}}(N)=\Theta\!\left(r\sum_{j=1}^{m}(jq)^2\right)=\Theta\!\left(\frac{rN^3}{q}\right).\] Peak representation storage is \(\Theta(Nr)\). Thus full retraining after frequent small batches can dominate a search even when the final factorization alone is affordable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly relearning a dense rank-r representation after small batches can accumulate cubic-in-data work, although the final representation uses only linear-times-rank storage.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Learning Overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits Representation-Learning Overhead. Given the stipulated Theta(n^2 r) retraining cost and integral N/q, the cumulative Theta(rN^3/q) calculation is correct. The result is algorithm-specific rather than a general representation-learning bound, and no source supports either the factorization model or its online-search interpretation.

children.title: Policy-Latency Overhead Coupling
children.top_down_role: Policy computation consuming a material share of the resource budget.

children.title: Decision Latency
children.top_down_role: Elapsed time between available evidence and the next evaluation decision.

assumptions_latex: An observation becomes available before the policy begins its next update.
Posterior updating, acquisition construction, acquisition optimization, and dispatch occur sequentially.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Decision latency is \(L_k=U_k+A_k+O_k+D_k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Latency is defined by additive accounting of sequential policy stages.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: End-to-end latency from observation availability to dispatch of the next evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For decision event \(k\), define the decision latency as the elapsed wall-clock time from availability of the triggering observation to dispatch of the selected next evaluation. Under sequential processing stages, \[L_k=U_k+A_k+O_k+D_k,\] where \(U_k\) is posterior-update time, \(A_k\) is acquisition-construction time, \(O_k\) is acquisition-optimization time, and \(D_k\) is scheduling and dispatch time. For parallel workers, the operational latency is the delay experienced by a worker that is ready but cannot receive a policy-consistent assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision latency is the wall-clock delay from receiving an observation to dispatching the next policy-selected evaluation, including update, acquisition, optimization, and scheduling time.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision Latency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Decision Latency, and the additive identity is valid under the explicitly sequential stages. No source is cited for this Bayesian-optimization latency definition. The final parallel-worker sentence introduces policy consistency and worker readiness without formal definitions, so its status as part of the same definition also requires clarification.

children.title: Policy Computation Overhead
children.top_down_role: Resource consumption attributable to policy evaluation and selection.

assumptions_latex: A search cycle performs serial policy computation of duration \(C_k\).
It then executes a synchronous batch whose evaluation duration is \(E_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Policy overhead fraction is \(h_k=C_k/(C_k+E_k)\), and it limits cycle speedup to \(1/h_k\) when only evaluations are accelerated.

notation.meaning: Serial policy-computation time in cycle k
Parallel evaluation time in cycle k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:The overhead fraction and speedup ceiling follow from serial-parallel cycle accounting.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Serial policy computation as a fraction of synchronous optimization-cycle time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For synchronous cycle \(k\), let policy computation take \(C_k\ge0\) time and parallel evaluation take \(E_k>0\) time. Define \[h_k=\frac{C_k}{C_k+E_k}.\] If evaluation is accelerated by a factor \(s\ge1\) while policy computation is unchanged, the cycle speedup is \[S_k(s)=\frac{C_k+E_k}{C_k+E_k/s}=\frac{1}{h_k+(1-h_k)/s}.\] Therefore \(\lim_{s\to\infty}S_k(s)=1/h_k\) whenever \(h_k>0\); policy computation ultimately bounds useful evaluation acceleration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Policy computation consumes a measurable share of each cycle and sets a finite speedup ceiling when only evaluations become faster.
knowledge_statements.title: Policy Computation Overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits Policy Computation Overhead, and the displayed speedup identity is correct. The assumptions allow C_k=0, hence h_k=0, while the conclusion_latex states a ceiling 1/h_k without its required h_k>0 qualification. The full statement supplies that qualification, creating an internal mismatch. No source is cited.

children.title: Budget-Share Regimes
children.top_down_role: Operating regimes distinguished by the policy computation share of total resources.

assumptions_latex: Total wall-clock budget at horizon \(N\) decomposes as \(B_N=C_N+E_N\).
Both policy-computation time \(C_N\) and evaluation time \(E_N\) are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limit behavior of \(\beta_N=C_N/B_N\) defines evaluation-dominated, balanced, and computation-dominated regimes.

notation.meaning: Total computation and evaluation times through horizon N

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:The regimes are a precise asymptotic classification of a two-part resource budget.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic regimes based on the wall-clock share consumed by policy computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_N=C_N+E_N>0\) be total wall-clock expenditure through \(N\) completed evaluations, and define the policy-computation share by \[\beta_N=\frac{C_N}{B_N}.\] The search is evaluation-dominated if \(\beta_N\to0\), balanced if \(\beta_N\to\beta\in(0,1)\), and computation-dominated if \(\beta_N\to1\). If the share has no limit, the corresponding regimes are expressed using \(\liminf\beta_N\) and \(\limsup\beta_N\); persistent balance requires both to lie strictly between \(0\) and \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Budget-share regimes classify a search by whether policy computation consumes a vanishing, nontrivial, or overwhelming fraction of total wall-clock time.
knowledge_statements.title: Budget-Share Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Budget-Share Regimes. The limiting and liminf/limsup classifications are mathematically coherent and plain text matches the LaTeX statement. Because the regime terminology is introduced without any citation, an inspectable source or an explicitly identified local convention is required.

children.title: Stale-Decision Consequences
children.top_down_role: Performance degradation when delayed decisions rely on outdated optimization state.

assumptions_latex: The acquisition \(a(x;P)\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in posterior state \(P\) under metric \(d\), uniformly over \(x\in X\).
The stale action is optimized within additive error \(\eta\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Using posterior \(P_s\) instead of \(P_f\) incurs fresh-acquisition loss at most \(2L d(P_s,P_f)+\eta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:The loss bound follows from uniform Lipschitz perturbation and approximate maximization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic acquisition-loss bound for decisions optimized against a stale posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(|a(x;P)-a(x;P')|\le Ld(P,P')\) for all \(x\in X\). Let \(x_s\) satisfy \(a(x_s;P_s)\ge\sup_x a(x;P_s)-\eta\), and let \(x_f\in\arg\max_x a(x;P_f)\). Then \[a(x_f;P_f)-a(x_s;P_f)\le 2L d(P_s,P_f)+\eta.\] Hence stale decisions are controlled when posterior drift is small. Without a finite sensitivity constant or a bound on posterior drift, arbitrarily small state changes may switch the maximizer and no nontrivial stale-decision guarantee follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stale posterior costs at most twice acquisition sensitivity times posterior drift, plus optimization error; without sensitivity control, no useful bound is available.
knowledge_statements.title: Stale-Decision Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits Stale-Decision Consequences, and the 2L d(P_s,P_f)+eta perturbation bound is standard once the stated approximate stale maximizer and a fresh maximizer exist. Existence of x_f in argmax is not guaranteed by the assumptions. The final no-guarantee assertion also needs a precisely quantified counterclass; maximizer switching alone does not establish large acquisition-value loss. No source is supplied.

children.title: Structure-Resource Misspecification Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between assumed structure, resource models, and the operating black box.

children.title: Incorrect Decomposition, Embedding, or Kernel Geometry
children.top_down_role: Representations excluding influential interactions, directions, or domain relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Incorrect Decomposition, Embedding, or Kernel Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses structural misspecification as exclusion of objective variation from the surrogate hypothesis class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be the design space, \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) the objective, and \(\mathcal H_{S}\) the function class induced by an assumed decomposition, embedding, or kernel geometry \(S\). The structure is incorrectly specified for \(f\) when \(f\notin\overline{\mathcal H_{S}}\), where closure is taken in the prediction norm used by the optimizer. Equivalently, the approximation error satisfies \[\varepsilon_S(f):=\inf_{g\in\mathcal H_S}\lVert f-g\rVert>0.\] Consequently, even exact inference within \(\mathcal H_S\) cannot reduce the surrogate error below \(\varepsilon_S(f)\); acquisition decisions may therefore systematically ignore influential interactions, directions, or domain relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural misspecification occurs when the assumed surrogate class cannot approximate the objective arbitrarily well, leaving an irreducible error that can misdirect acquisition decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\neq\varnothing\) and the prediction norm is defined on functions over \(\mathcal X\).
\(\mathcal H_S\) is the hypothesis class imposed by the selected structural representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\notin\overline{\mathcal H_S}\Longrightarrow \varepsilon_S(f)>0\).

notation.meaning: assumed decomposition, embedding, or kernel geometry
surrogate hypothesis class induced by S

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences
source_refs.locator: 2.1.2 Sequential design and nonstationary surrogate modeling p. 34

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: positive distance from the imposed hypothesis class is the standard approximation-theoretic boundary for structural misspecification

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences
source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.2 Sequential design and nonstationary surrogate modeling p. 34

children.title: Unknown-Structure Identifiability
children.top_down_role: Insufficient evidence to distinguish competing structural explanations.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Structure Identifiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses observational equivalence to characterize whether competing surrogate structures can be distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak S\) be a set of candidate structures and let \(P_S^\pi\) denote the probability law of the complete observation history generated under structure \(S\) and sampling policy \(\pi\). A true structure \(S_0\in\mathfrak S\) is identifiable under \(\pi\) precisely when \[P_S^\pi=P_{S_0}^\pi\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S=S_0\] for every \(S\in\mathfrak S\), up to any declared structural equivalence. Unknown-structure identifiability fails when distinct, nonequivalent structures \(S_1\neq S_2\) induce the same history law. In that case no estimator based solely on that history can distinguish \(S_1\) from \(S_2\) with vanishing error under both models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structure is identifiable when no distinct admissible structure produces the same observation-history law; observationally equivalent structures cannot be consistently distinguished.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathfrak S\) is the declared candidate structure class.
\(P_S^\pi\) includes evaluation locations, outcomes, failures, and completion information observed by policy \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_0\) is identifiable under \(\pi\) if and only if its observational-equivalence class is a singleton.

notation.meaning: law of the observed adaptive history under structure S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: injectivity of the observable-law map is the standard statistical definition of identifiability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The observable-law injectivity condition is mathematically standard and fits the identifiability leaf, but no inspectable citation supports the adaptive-history formulation or the impossibility statement for estimators.

children.title: Resource-Prediction Error Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Allocation distortions caused by inaccurate resource models.

children.title: Cost Prediction Error
children.top_down_role: Allocation effects of inaccurate monetary or resource-cost forecasts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost Prediction Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines pointwise and integrated discrepancy between predicted and conditional expected evaluation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(x)\geq0\) be the random resource cost of evaluating design \(x\in\mathcal X\), and let \(\widehat c(x)\) be a predictor based on the current history. With \(c(x):=\mathbb E[C(x)\mid x]\), the signed cost-prediction error is \[e_c(x):=\widehat c(x)-c(x).\] For a design distribution \(\mu\), its root-mean-square magnitude is \[E_c(\mu):=\left(\int_{\mathcal X}e_c(x)^2\,\mu(dx)\right)^{1/2},\] whenever the integral is finite. Positive error represents expected-cost overprediction and negative error represents expected-cost underprediction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cost prediction error is the difference between predicted evaluation cost and true conditional expected cost, measured pointwise or under a design distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(C(x)\) is integrable for each relevant \(x\).
\(\widehat c\) is measurable and square-integrable under \(\mu\) when \(E_c(\mu)\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_c(x)=0\) exactly when the predicted and conditional expected costs agree at \(x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise and fits the cost-prediction leaf, but the cited section on modeling time does not clearly support evaluation-cost prediction or the proposed integrated error measure. A directly relevant forecasting or cost-aware optimization source is required.

children.title: Runtime Prediction Error
children.top_down_role: Scheduling effects of inaccurate evaluation-duration forecasts.

knowledge_statements.title: Runtime Prediction Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines discrepancy between predicted and conditional expected completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(x)\geq0\) be the random runtime of evaluating \(x\in\mathcal X\), and let \(\widehat\tau(x)\) be a history-measurable runtime predictor. If \(\tau(x):=\mathbb E[T(x)\mid x]\) is finite, the signed runtime-prediction error is \[e_T(x):=\widehat\tau(x)-\tau(x).\] For a design distribution \(\mu\), an aggregate absolute error is \[E_T(\mu):=\int_{\mathcal X}|e_T(x)|\,\mu(dx),\] provided the integral exists. Thus \(e_T(x)<0\) denotes underprediction of expected runtime and \(e_T(x)>0\) denotes overprediction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime prediction error compares predicted completion time with true conditional expected runtime; its sign distinguishes underprediction from overprediction.
assumptions_latex: \(T(x)\) has finite conditional mean at each relevant design.
\(\widehat\tau\) is measurable with respect to information available before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_T(x)=0\) exactly when \(\widehat\tau(x)=\mathbb E[T(x)\mid x]\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: prediction error is defined as forecast minus conditional target

children.title: Allocation Distortion
children.top_down_role: Resource assignment failures induced by prediction error.

knowledge_statements.title: Allocation Distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies resource-allocation changes induced by erroneous predicted costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a^*\in\mathcal A\) minimize the true allocation objective \(L(a;c)\), where \(c\) is the vector of expected evaluation costs, and let \(\widehat a\in\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal A}L(a;\widehat c)\) be the allocation selected using predicted costs \(\widehat c\). The decision distortion and realized allocation loss are respectively \[D_{\mathcal A}(\widehat c,c):=d(\widehat a,a^*)\quad\text{and}\quad R_{\mathcal A}(\widehat c,c):=L(\widehat a;c)-L(a^*;c)\geq0.\] Allocation distortion occurs when either quantity is positive, even if the underlying objective surrogate is correctly specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocation distortion measures how predicted resource costs change the chosen allocation and how much true allocation performance is consequently lost.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is nonempty and both optimization problems attain minima.
\(d\) is a metric or declared decision discrepancy on \(\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\mathcal A}(\widehat c,c)\geq0\), with strict inequality whenever \(\widehat a\) is not truly optimal and the optimum is strict.

notation.meaning: allocation objective evaluated with true costs

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: decision distortion and plug-in regret are standard consequences of parameter misspecification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The plug-in decision discrepancy and realized loss fit the allocation-distortion leaf, and the nonnegativity conclusion follows from true optimality. No inspectable source supports this particular resource-allocation sensitivity formulation.

children.title: Resource-Model Calibration Failures
children.top_down_role: Operating conditions where predicted resource demands cease to support reliable allocation.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Model Calibration Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes failure of probabilistic resource forecasts to match conditional event frequencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each design \(x\in\mathcal X\), let \(F_x(t)\) be the predictive distribution function for a resource variable \(R(x)\), and define \(U:=F_X(R(X))\), using randomized probability-integral transforms when atoms occur. The resource model is probabilistically calibrated under design law \(\mu\) when \[\mathbb P(U\leq u)=u\quad\text{for every }u\in[0,1],\quad X\sim\mu.\] A calibration failure occurs when some \(u\) violates this equality. Conditional calibration failure occurs when the equality fails after conditioning on a declared design or context group, even if the marginal equality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource model fails calibration when its forecast probabilities do not match observed conditional frequencies, globally or within relevant design groups.
assumptions_latex: \(R(x)\) is observable for completed evaluations.
\(F_x\) is a measurable predictive distribution available before observing \(R(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists u\in[0,1]:\mathbb P(U\leq u)\neq u\) certifies marginal calibration failure.

notation.meaning: random resource consumption at design x

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The probability-integral-transform criterion is a valid marginal probabilistic-calibration condition and the failure-boundary kind fits. The cited computer-model calibration section appears to concern parameter calibration rather than probabilistic forecast calibration, so a directly supporting source is required.

children.title: Runtime Tail-Shift Regimes
children.top_down_role: Completion behavior poorly summarized by ordinary runtime models.

children.title: Heavy-Tailed Runtime
children.top_down_role: Completion behavior dominated by rare, exceptionally long evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tailed Runtime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines heavy runtime tails by absence of a finite exponential moment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a design \(x\in\mathcal X\), let \(T(x)\geq0\) denote evaluation runtime. The runtime distribution is heavy-tailed at \(x\) when \[\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda T(x))\mid x]=\infty\quad\text{for every }\lambda>0.\] A runtime family is uniformly heavy-tailed on \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\) when this condition holds for every \(x\in A\). This definition allows finite or infinite mean runtime; if additionally \(\mathbb P(T(x)>t)=t^{-\alpha}\ell(t)\) for a slowly varying \(\ell\), then the tail is regularly varying with index \(-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime is heavy-tailed when no positive exponential moment exists; regularly varying runtime tails form an important subclass.
assumptions_latex: \(T(x)\) is a nonnegative random variable for each relevant design.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Heavy-tailed runtime excludes every exponential-tail bound derived from a finite positive moment-generating function.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nonexistence of all positive exponential moments is a standard definition of a heavy-tailed distribution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Absence of every positive exponential moment is a standard heavy-tail condition and fits the leaf, but the record has no inspectable source for either that definition or the regularly varying subclass.

children.title: Nonstationary Runtime
children.top_down_role: Completion behavior whose distribution changes during optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonstationary Runtime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines runtime nonstationarity through changing conditional laws across launch time or system state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_n(x)\) be the runtime of the \(n\)-th evaluation launched at design \(x\), and let \(Z_n\) denote its observed system context. Runtime is stationary relative to \(Z_n\) when there exists a kernel \(Q(\cdot\mid x,z)\), independent of \(n\), such that \[\mathcal L(T_n(x)\mid x,Z_n=z)=Q(\cdot\mid x,z)\] for all relevant \(n,x,z\). It is nonstationary when no such time-invariant kernel exists; equivalently, some fixed \(x,z\) and indices \(m\neq n\) have unequal conditional runtime laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime is nonstationary when its conditional distribution changes over evaluation index or calendar time after controlling for the declared context.
assumptions_latex: \(T_n(x)\) and the declared context \(Z_n\) are jointly measurable.
Comparisons use contexts having positive probability or a specified regular conditional law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x,z,m\neq n:\mathcal L(T_m(x)\mid x,Z_m=z)\neq\mathcal L(T_n(x)\mid x,Z_n=z)\) implies nonstationary runtime.

notation.meaning: runtime of evaluation n at design x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stationarity requires invariance of the declared conditional law over time

children.title: Tail-Shift Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Runtime settings combining extreme-duration risk with temporal distribution shifts.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Shift Interaction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates runtime-law changes into tail changes, context shifts, and their interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\in\{0,1\}\) index two operating regimes and let \(Z\) be context. For thresholds \(t\), define the conditional survival function \(\overline F_s(t\mid x,z):=\mathbb P(T>t\mid X=x,Z=z,S=s)\). A tail-shift interaction is present when the regime tail ratio \[\rho(t,x,z):=\frac{\overline F_1(t\mid x,z)}{\overline F_0(t\mid x,z)}\] is not constant in \(x\) or \(z\) over the declared tail range. Thus the runtime-tail shift cannot be represented solely by a regime-wide multiplicative factor; its severity depends on design or context.
